I leaned in. In the mirrored depth of the false wall, behind the smiling faces, barely distinguishable in the blur, stood a man. A figure in a dark suit, very far off, almost out of frame. He wasn't looking at the photographer. He was looking straight at me — with a heavy, fixed stare.
"In the very corner of the print," I turned the photo and tapped a nail against a purple stamp. "Look."
Camden Analog Lab. 1994 — the founding year, stamped right into the die. An old photo lab that had somehow, miraculously, gone on surviving in the basements of Camden Market…
"This is our first real lead," I said. "Whoever brought this photo to my door had it printed there. You can't pull that kind of depth of field out of a reflection from a digital file. It needed a physical negative."
Helen nodded, not taking her eyes off the stamp.
"Tomorrow morning."
"Tomorrow morning," I agreed.
She stayed the night. There was nowhere for her to go — by then her own flat was registered to an unfamiliar name, and any hotel would require an identity verification that no longer existed in any database. We talked for a few more hours — quietly, without turning on the overhead light. Then we fell silent. I could hear her breathing in the dark of the living room, and for some reason that was the one thing, out of this entire endless day, that felt real to me.
Close to midnight, a sound came from deep in the hallway.
A rattling, mechanical, double strike of a bell.
Brring-brring.
We both froze, barely breathing. The sound was coming from the dusty corner behind the coat rack. An old rotary phone from the eighties. A heavy black Bakelite unit, left behind by the previous tenants. It wasn't even hooked up to anything modern — a thick grey cord ran off somewhere into the skirting board. Not a single person I knew had that number. I didn't even know it myself.
Brring-brring.
I walked slowly to the little table. Picked up the heavy receiver. Pressed it to my ear.
Absolute, dead silence filled the line. No dial tone, no static. As if I were listening to the emptiness of space.
And then, out of that emptiness, a man's voice came — dry, flat, without a trace of intonation:
"Ask Harris… what happened on the sixteenth of October."
A short metallic click. The line went dead.
I slowly set the receiver back on its cradle. Turned to Helen. She was looking at me, her hands still gripping the collar of her coat.
"Which year?" she asked quietly.
I said nothing. We'd both understood the worst part at the exact same moment.
The voice on the line hadn't named a year. It was certain we already knew we ought to remember.

title: Chapter 10
body:
We left the flat before dawn.
Without a word — at some point we both simply understood we wouldn't be sleeping anymore, and got dressed in silence. We rode the tube to Camden without talking. The carriage was almost empty — just a cleaner in an orange vest dozing at the far end, and an elderly woman with a shopping bag staring into the black glass of the window. London at this early hour felt like a different city — quiet, not yet having pulled on its daytime indifference.
We reached the lab a little after eight. Locked. Someone had marked the opening hour on the door in felt-tip — ten. We went back into the alley and found a small greasy spoon on the corner — nameless, with cracked plastic chairs, and eggs that we both ate in silence, forks moving mechanically. An old fridge rattled behind us, a television muttered on the wall without sound. An ordinary, deeply mundane scene.
It was here that something happened I hadn't expected at all.
Helen picked up her knife and fork with confidence, tried to separate a piece of fish, and hit a thick spine bone. The fish slid off, and a chunk of batter landed with a wet slap right in the tartar sauce, splashing her collar. She froze, fork raised, a tiny scrap of fish dangling forlornly off the end.
I couldn't hold it in and let out a quiet snort of laughter.
"This isn't funny, Lawson," she said sternly, but her lips were already twitching. "They don't teach you how to dissect street food in the ministry's archival manuals."
"You have to go old-school," I took the cutlery from her, grabbed a clean napkin, and pulled out the long white bone with my fingers. "There. No automation. Pure analog."
Helen laughed, suddenly, genuinely, head thrown back. All her strict, tightly-wound composure evaporated for a second, and in front of me was simply a very exhausted woman who, for the first time in days, had let herself relax. I watched her and thought: we're alive. And we damn well want to stay that way.
"All right, engineer," she smiled, wiping her fingers with the napkin. "Time to go."
The sign we were looking for — Camden Analog Lab. Photo & Film — turned up in a half-basement, reached by a steep stone stairway with chipped steps. No neon, no screens. Just a dim yellow bulb over a heavy door and a cracked shop window, behind which sat dusty empty film spools and yellowed samples of photo paper.
An old bell chimed overhead as we stepped through the door. Inside it smelled of chemicals — a sharp, sour, nose-tingling smell of fixer and developer. That smell cut off the modern world instantly.
The owner came out from behind a heavy wool curtain. He was in his seventies. Thin grey hair combed back, round glasses in a cheap horn frame on his nose, and fingers stained with the characteristic yellow-brown marks of years of working with chemicals.
"Morning," he smiled warmly, wiping his hands on a canvas apron. "Film? I can only take it for developing this evening, just poured fresh chemicals. Hardly anyone prints from film by hand these days. Everyone's gone digital, into their phones… And there's no soul in those, you know? Just pixels. But here — it's substance."
"We're not here to develop anything," I took the glossy photo out of my pocket and set it on the wooden counter. "We need to find out who printed this. And when."
The old man pulled out a second, stronger pair of glasses and bent over the photograph.
"Ohh," he clicked his tongue approvingly. "Nice work. Kodak Premier paper, mid-nineties, excellent contrast. They don't make it like this anymore."
He flipped the print over and his eyes landed straight on the purple stamp in the corner. His face lit up with a childlike pride.
"Well, of course. That's my stamp. See this tiny nick on the 'L'? I dropped the die on the stone floor by accident back in '96. Yes, young man. This photograph was printed here. In this very lab."
Something inside me pulled taut. The photograph was real. No neural network had conjured it up overnight. A physical human being had made it, in this basement.
"We need the client's name," Helen stepped forward, palms flat on the counter. "Please. It's a matter of life and death."
The old man sighed and reached under the counter. With a dull thud, he pulled out an enormous, thick book bound in rough leatherette. The order ledger. Paper, worn, its yellowed pages filled with handwriting in different hands. Pencil, blue ink, black gel pen. No computers.
"We don't throw out our archives," he muttered, turning the thick pages. The rustle of paper in the silence of the basement seemed deafening. "Systems break, disks get wiped, but paper just sits there. Right, five years ago… October…"
He ran a finger down the lines. I held my breath.
"Here. Order number 4082. Specification: hand print from a 35mm negative, enlargement, high-contrast paper. Date of pickup… the sixteenth of October."
Helen and I looked at each other.
"Who's the client?" I asked quickly.
The old man frowned. He pulled the ledger closer to his eyes, and his good-natured smile slowly faded.
I leaned over and looked at the open page. There was no entry in the "Client Name" field. And it wasn't a matter of ink. Someone had carefully, with surgical precision, cut a rectangular piece out of the paper with a sharp blade. Clean, even edges. Absolute emptiness where the name should be. Whatever was wiping us out of electronic registries didn't know how to clean paper this neatly — someone else, physical, with their own hands and a scalpel, had done this work by hand.
"Strange…" the old man said quietly. He touched the hole in the page with a finger. "I remember filling this line in. I remember that day. A young man came in, brought the film in a black tube. I remember what he was wearing. A dark coat, expensive… But I… God, I can't remember his face."
His voice trembled. An ordinary man, far removed from our nightmare, had suddenly run into a blank wall inside his own head. Fine beads of sweat appeared on his forehead.
"I can't remember his face," he repeated, panic rising in his voice. "It's like there's… just a grey smear there. Must be my age. Right? Just a lapse of memory…"
A chill ran through me. Whatever this was, it reached beyond registries and databases — it reached into the memory of perfectly ordinary people, erasing not lines in a computer but neural connections inside someone else's head.
"It's all right," Helen gently touched the old man's hand. "It's just tiredness. Thank you."
He was quiet for a moment, staring at the counter, then raised his head.
"The lab has a negative archive," he said. "If the negative's still here, we can find it by the order number. But it'll take time. Come back tomorrow morning — I'll close the shop and we'll go down to the archive together."
While we were talking at the counter, a man walked into the shop. Perfectly ordinary. Grey raincoat, cap, a face so unremarkable you'd forget it a second later. He just stood by the entrance, looked at us, bought nothing, and left. When I asked the owner if he knew him, he said: "No. But that's the second time he's come in today."
We left at seven. The owner flipped the sign to "Closed" and turned the key in the lock. We stood on the opposite side of the street, watching the lights go out in the basement windows.
"We're being watched," Helen said quietly. "We're being tracked."
"Yes," I answered.
We walked a couple of blocks and turned toward the tube. We didn't see that, about five minutes after we'd left, the old man went back into the dark shop — he'd remembered leaving his glasses on the counter. He knew the way by heart and didn't switch on the light. He felt for the arms of his glasses, but his eyes happened to fall on the open leatherette ledger. He remembered clearly closing it and putting it away under the counter.
The book lay open. Right on the page from October, five years back. The very page with the neat rectangular hole gaping where the name had been cut out.
Right beside that hole, in the clean margin of the page, someone had just left a fresh note. The letters were traced in a neat, firm pencil stroke. The graphite still gleamed faintly in the dim light from the streetlamp.
A single line, written without a single smudge:
You're looking for the wrong man.
The old man slowly raised his head, scanning the empty, lifeless room. No one. Just the quiet rustle of a draft at the door and the distant rumble of Camden Market.
When we came back the next morning, he met us at the door — pale, glasses in hand — and told us everything.

title: Chapter 11
body:
Why 'the wrong man,' specifically?
That question turned over in my head the whole way back to Camden. All night, while Helen and I sat in my living room, the line left in pencil on the margin of the order ledger felt like more than a warning. It shifted the whole frame of reference. Whoever was tailing us wasn't trying to confuse us. He was trying to tear the blinders off.
We'd latched onto the photograph as a lead only because it had been left under my door with a stranger's face circled in marker. But what if that was staged too?
The wrong man compared to whom?
The morning met us with a thick, motionless fog, rare for a London June. The old photographer was waiting at the door of the lab — pale, glasses in hand. He told us about the note in the ledger straight away. His voice shook slightly — not from fear, more from the kind of bewilderment people get when their familiar reality suddenly turns out thinner than they'd thought.
Inside, the shop was exactly as before. The usual smell of chemicals, two mugs of strong instant coffee steaming on the table, made ready by the old man for our arrival. The heavy order book lay in place — open to that same page. The pencil line looked completely ordinary in daylight. But it was precisely that ordinariness that frightened me most.
"We won't be able to get down to the archive," the old man held up his yellowed palms. "Not right now. A main pipe burst in the alley overnight. Our basement section flooded. Not badly, three inches or so, but it came in right along the left wall, where the boxes from the nineties are."
I froze on the first step of the stairs down to the basement.
"You're joking," my voice came out quieter than I meant it to.
"No joke about it," the old man sighed and straightened his glasses. "The insurance is already on its way, the assessor will be here by noon. I need to move the top shelves to a dry spot before the cardboard soaks through. Life doesn't stop for other people's mysteries. I've got forty years of archive down there."
No men in black masks. No elegant break-in. Just a rusted-out pipe and stinking tap water. An ordinary domestic disaster, completely indifferent to the fact that you're trying to save your own life.
Something inside me snapped.
"Why does it happen every single time?!" I lost it, slamming a hand against the wooden banister hard enough to shake loose a century of dust. "Every time we get close, some stupid, absurd coincidence blocks our way! The phone, the database, now a damn pipe!"
I expected Helen to try to calm me down. Cut me off, call me back to logic. But she didn't even glance my way. She silently took off her heavy coat, hung it carefully on the hook by the door, rolled the sleeves of her grey blouse up to the elbows, and went down into the damp, dim basement. A moment later a heavy shuffling sound came up from below — she was dragging the first waterlogged cardboard box toward the stairs.
I looked at her straight, tense back. My anger evaporated instantly, leaving shame in its place. I shrugged off my coat and went down after her.
For the next hour we worked in complete, dead silence. Passing heavy boxes down a chain, smelling of damp and old celluloid, stacking them on the dry shelves along the right wall. The basement air was thick and cold, and our feet were quickly soaked in the stale water. It was our first real joint effort — not an exchange of information, just the plain physical labor of two people stuck together in the same darkness.
Somewhere around the thirtieth box, the bottom of an old cardboard cube gave out. The soaked seam split, and glossy envelopes and old negatives spilled out with a rustle, straight into the dirty water on the concrete floor.
"Oh, sorry," the old man, standing above, threw up his hands. "That's a very old corner, fifteen years or so. Not your boxes, leave them, I'll pick them up later…"
I was already crouched down, instinctively fishing translucent film sleeves out of the water before the damp ruined the prints for good. My fingers moved on autopilot, until my eyes caught on one of the negatives.
I froze. Water dripped off my fingers, but I didn't notice the cold.
I lifted the strip of film to eye level, catching the dim light of the bare bulb. A negative always gives you those first few seconds of disorientation — light and shadow swapping places, faces turning into white masks. I held the film until the inverted shadows resolved into familiar shapes — and then I recognized it.
A huge banquet hall. The same semicircular sweep of panoramic windows. The same parquet pattern. The same massive columns of the Radisson. But the people were different. Different faces, a different occasion, a different decade — you could tell from the small things, the haircuts, the cut of the jackets. A completely different event. The same hall.
But right at the edge of the frame, by the mirrored wall, a familiar silhouette showed.
"Helen," I called quietly. "The loupe. Now."
She was beside me instantly. I climbed out of the water, went up to the counter, and laid the two prints side by side: our glossy five-year-old print from yesterday, and this wet, faded negative from almost forty years ago.
Under the magnifying glass, the gap in years dissolved. The hall was identical. The faces of the guests in the foreground shifted like frames in a kaleidoscope — decades shuffling their fates, their names, their fashions, their eras. But back there, deep in the frame, by the reflective glass, the same figure stood in both photographs. The exact same build. The same tilt of the head. The same fixed, unmoving gaze, aimed not at the celebrating crowd but at the camera lens itself. He had no face — on the old film it had dissolved into a blurred dark smudge from the contrast — but the geometry of his body was frighteningly unchanged.
The five-year-old photograph wasn't unique. The observer was.
This man had been standing there for years. Possibly decades. He'd been present at every key turning point, while the reality around him kept shifting over and over. And the anonymous pencil note now took on a bone-chilling meaning: we'd been looking at the wrong man.
The old photographer stepped closer, studying the wet plastic in my hands. He was quiet for a long while, listening to the steady drip of water in the corner of the basement.
"You know," he said quietly, and a strange, deep sorrow cut through his voice. "I used to know every regular customer by face. Every one. Remembered who had which camera, who liked which paper. And now… faces just float past. Like water."
His words dropped into the silence of the room heavier than any manifesto. Whatever was happening wasn't just erasing data in registries — it was erasing human attachment itself.
Helen slowly lowered the loupe. Her fingers were still stained with grey basement dust.
"Do you remember the sixteenth of October?" she asked, looking the old man straight in the eye. "Five years ago. The day that order was collected."
The old man thought for a long time. Took off his glasses, rubbed the bridge of his nose. Something in his head was straining to turn, grinding against invisible blocks.
"I don't know," he said slowly. "Not because the box got wet. I simply, physically can't remember whether I printed anything that day at all. My head's blank. As if that day simply wasn't part of my autumn."
His own memory, right now, was becoming evidence — or rather, its complete, forced absence was.
"We should go," Helen said quietly, pulling on her coat. "There's nothing more to pull out of here."
We'd already reached the door, the bell overhead about to ring, when the old man suddenly called out to us from behind the counter:
"Young man! Wait."
I turned. The photographer stood with his hands braced on the wooden edge of the counter, his eyes wide, his breathing quick. As if he'd just pulled a single, miraculously surviving fragment out of a drowning mind.
"I remembered one detail," he breathed out. "That young man… the client in the dark coat. The sixteenth of October. He didn't come alone."
I took two steps back into the shop, feeling everything inside me clench.
"Who was with him?"
The old man closed his eyes. His face contorted with extreme, agonized effort. At least a full minute of ringing silence passed. Finally he slowly opened his eyes and looked at us with a deep, almost childlike bewilderment.
"I can't see a face," he said quietly. "Not at all. But I… I remember the sound of her laugh. Bright, dry… She was laughing at some joke. I know for certain it was a woman. But her face… it's simply not there."
The shop went very quiet. Just the steady drip from the basement.
I slowly turned to Helen.
She stood motionless, coat in her hands. Her face was completely impassive — that same professional blankness I'd already learned to recognize as a warning sign. That was how she'd looked in the bunker, when she found her own name in the ledger. Something was happening beneath that stillness — something she wasn't ready to say out loud.
Bright, dry laughter.
A few minutes ago, at that greasy spoon over eggs, that was exactly how she'd laughed. Head thrown back, genuine, bright. I remembered it. I'd just heard that exact sound.
She'd heard it too. I could see it in how she held her coat — too tightly, with both hands, as if she needed something to hold onto.
"Thank you," she told the old man, her voice level. "You've helped us a great deal."
We stepped outside. The bell chimed behind us. The fog had lifted a little by then, but hadn't cleared — it had simply risen higher, hanging somewhere above the rooftops, turning the sky into a white, matte nothing.
We walked in silence. For a long time. Past the canal, past the market, past tourists with maps in hand who glanced at us and immediately stopped looking.
Helen was the first to stop at the parapet above the water.
"I don't remember that day," she finally said, without turning around. "The sixteenth of October, five years ago. I don't remember that autumn at all. I thought it was just… that everyone has blank spots. That I was just tired back then."
She fell silent for a moment.
"But I just realized I don't remember a single day of that autumn. Not one."
The water below was dark and still. Somewhere far off, a river ferry sounded its horn.
"Helen," I said carefully.
"Don't," she shook her head. "I know what you're about to say. Don't."
She was quiet again. Then she turned to face me after all, and there was something in her eyes I hadn't seen there before — not fear, not anger, but something far quieter, and for that, far more frightening.
"So I was there," she said evenly. "Next to the one who brought the film. On that exact day. And I was laughing."
She turned back to the water.
And I don't remember why at all.

title: Chapter 12
body:
If Thomas Harris wasn't the central figure in this conspiracy, then why had someone worked so hard to cut him out of my life? Why had a stranger's hand circled his face in red marker on an archive photograph?
On the overground train heading toward south London, we sat in silence. Neither of us brought up the old photographer's last words. A woman with a bright, dry laugh, whose face had dissolved out of a stranger's memory and left only a sonic ghost behind — that detail frightened me precisely because it was so intangible. Witnesses' memory was turning into too unstable a swamp. Something was changing it on the fly, right while we were asking questions.
Harris, on the other hand, was tangible. He was flesh and blood. We needed to look for his private, unofficial past — not in the City, where reality had already been rewritten and armored behind corporate bureaucracy.
Helen opened her bag and pulled out a small notebook bound in worn leather. Paper again. No notes app on a phone, no cloud storage. Just her small, cramped ballpoint handwriting on yellowed pages. She leafed through it for a long time, the pages rustling under the monotonous clatter of the wheels.
"I think I found his old address after all," she said, not looking up. "Five years old. From before he moved to Kensington. This house belonged to his family."
We got off at a quiet, sleepy station in Clapham. An ordinary, comfortable residential area. Two-story Victorian brick terraces, clean pavements. Further off, on a patch of park lawn, kids in school uniforms shrieked as they played, a man in a tracksuit lazily walked a golden retriever, and a delivery courier, having parked his van right at the intersection, swore furiously at his sat nav. Ordinary, unhurried life went on flowing as it always did. This whole neighborhood, all this mundane, drowsy normalcy — it knew nothing about what was happening to us, and it was precisely that total obliviousness that offered a thin, fragile hope.
An elderly woman opened the door of the house we were looking for. She wore a woolen cardigan, and from deep in the hallway came the smell of dried lavender and mint tea. A distant relative of Harris's, looking after the house, which Thomas now rented out.
She knew Thomas. Yes. He really had lived here for years, before his business took off.
I couldn't help smiling with relief, feeling the tension drain out of my shoulders. Finally. A living witness whose memory hadn't glitched yet.
And then, straightening the collar of her cardigan, the woman said, in a perfectly ordinary voice:
"You know… it's almost funny. You're the second person to ask me about Thomas this week."
My smile froze instantly. The air in the hallway seemed to turn colder at once.
"Who was the first one?" Helen took half a step forward, her voice quiet but ringing with steel.
The woman frowned, looking somewhere over our heads.
"Oh, I… I don't remember," she spread her hands helplessly. "His face has just gone clean out of my head. You know, at my age… But it was definitely a man. In a dark coat. Stood on the doorstep, asked if any of Thomas's old papers were still here, and left."
Helen and I exchanged a glance. That same grey figure from Camden. He wasn't just following us — he was operating in parallel, checking the same key points, staying one step ahead of us.
"But I didn't give him anything," the woman went on, smiling weakly. "Thomas had asked me to keep something of his. Said he'd pick it up when he moved out for good, and then just forgot about it for five years. And I don't let strangers into the house. You're his colleagues, aren't you? You're from him?"
I nodded quickly, before Helen could get a word in:
"Yes. He asked us to pick it up."
A couple of minutes later she brought out of the closet a small shoebox, coated in a thick layer of grey dust, tied with yellowed string.
There was nothing sensational inside the box. No encrypted drives, no documents stamped classified. Just the ordinary, touching debris of a human life. An old cashmere scarf, a couple of paperback detective novels, a few cassette tapes of old rock records, a stack of yellowed supermarket receipts and electricity bills. It was exactly this mundane, domestic sloppiness that made the box's contents absolutely, irrefutably real. It would never occur to anyone to doctor an old receipt for a carton of milk.
I sorted carefully through the items until my fingers hit something hard and plastic at the very bottom.
A cheap, disposable Kodak camera in a yellow-and-blue plastic body. The frame counter was frozen at "24." The whole roll had been shot. But no one had ever developed it.
I turned the camera over — and felt a roughness under my fingers. On the grey plastic of the battery cover, something sharp had scratched two Latin letters, carelessly.
Small, almost invisible unless you knew where to look.
M. L.
They weren't Thomas Harris's initials.
They were mine. And I knew that uneven, slightly left-leaning hand far too well. It was my own.
I'd scratched those letters into this camera myself.
But I remembered absolutely nothing, not a trace, about when or why I'd done it.
On my palm lay a camera I'd held five years ago. One I'd given to Harris myself for safekeeping — and had no memory of it. Our past with him had been stitched together with a shared thread long before anyone started their cleanup. We'd been at the same point. On the same day. And the price of that day was locked inside this cheap piece of plastic.
Out on the street, Helen stopped, coat in hand. I held the camera out to her. She took it between two fingers, examined the initials, ran the pad of her thumb over them — the way you touch something you want to remember by feel.
"You gave it to him yourself," she said. Not a question.
"Yes," I answered. "I must have known, back then, that I couldn't keep it with me."
We were quiet for a moment. A woman with a double pram passed without looking at us. From the distance came the laughter of children in the park.
"We don't need to go back to the photographer," Helen finally said, tucking the camera into her bag. "Not yet. If you wrote 'don't develop' yourself — we need to understand why, first."
I nodded.
We walked toward the station. In my pocket I carried the shoebox with its stack of old receipts and the cashmere scarf that had once belonged to a man I apparently knew far better than I could remember.

title: Chapter 13
body:
In the morning I didn't go to any lab.
Instead I made coffee — real coffee, in an old stovetop moka pot I found at the back of a kitchen drawer, one I hadn't used in about three years — poured it into the one surviving porcelain cup, and sat down at the table. I set the yellow plastic rectangle of the camera down in front of me. And just started looking at it.
Not as a mystery. As evidence.
That's how investigators work a crime scene when they're not in a hurry. They don't grab the first object they find and rush it to a lab. They sit and look. For a long time. Patiently. Letting the object tell them things about itself it doesn't even suspect it's telling.
The camera was cheap. An early-2000s Kodak Precision — the kind that cost three pounds at a petrol station and sold next to chewing gum and car air fresheners. The plastic body had yellowed and picked up light scratches, but not from age — from careless storage. The frame counter read "24." The whole roll had been shot. Someone had pressed that button twenty-four times, peering through the tiny viewfinder — and then put the camera in a shoebox and never touched it again.
That someone was me.
I took a sip of coffee. Set the cup down. Kept looking.
A person who photographs something on film wants to preserve it. But a person who photographs something on film and then never develops it wants something else. He wants to preserve a possibility. He wants the information to exist — but stay inaccessible. Locked away. Hidden behind a chemical barrier that requires a deliberate act to cross.
This wasn't forgetfulness. It was a strategy.
I threw on a jacket, took the camera, and went out.
I found the shop I needed two blocks away — a tiny basement photo-supply store with a faded sign reading "Batteries. Film. Repairs," squeezed between a dry cleaner's and a nail salon. A bell dangled over the entrance — just like the one at the photographer's in Camden, only smaller and higher-pitched. Behind the counter sat a man in his sixties with a thick grey beard, reading a newspaper folded into quarters.
I set the camera down in front of him.
"Not for developing," I said right away. "I have a question."
He looked up from the paper.
"How long can exposed film keep? In a camera like this, somewhere dark, at room temperature?"
The man picked up the camera, turned it over in his hands with that professional indifference that comes from years of familiarity with objects, and set it back down.
"Dark and dry — decades," he said simply. "Color degrades, but black and white holds up for a long time. Kodak Precision's black-and-white stock, by the way. So if there's something on it, it's still there."
"Thanks," I put the camera back in my pocket.
The man was already reaching for his newspaper.
"One more question," I added. "If someone deliberately doesn't develop an exposed roll for years — what's usually the reason?"
He thought about it for a second.
"Either they forgot," he said. "Or they were afraid of seeing what's on it."
I nodded and went outside. Sat down on a bench in the tiny square across the street, took out the camera, and held it again.
Five years in the dark, and it was intact. I'd put it there myself. I'd written "don't develop" myself. I'd given it to Harris myself and asked him to hide it — in a box, among old receipts and cassettes, somewhere no one would deliberately look.
Except there was one thing I couldn't work out: was this camera waiting for me. Or for someone else.
That same morning, while I sat on the bench, Helen had already spent several hours in the reading room of a government archive in Westminster, methodically working through five-year-old payroll ledgers for Harris & Croft.
The archive smelled the way every archive in the world smells — dry dust, old binding glue, a faint chemical bitterness from preservative compounds. The reading room was empty — besides Helen, only an elderly man in a tweed jacket sat there, copying something out by hand into a notebook, pages rustling quietly now and then. The fluorescent lights overhead hummed on, monotonous, almost meditative.
It was endlessly tedious, exhausting work. The kind they never show in films.
Helen wrote names into her notebook in a column. Each name its own line, position and department beside it, the signature under the ledger entry. She was reconstructing the company's staffing structure from that autumn the way a restorer reconstructs a faded fresco — carefully, layer by layer, unhurried, missing nothing.
By midday the picture was nearly complete. Nearly.
Right at the end of the fourth section — IT and external contractors — she stopped.
Line forty-seven. Employee number — present. Department — present. Salary grade — present. Contract dates — present. Signature confirming receipt of pay — present. And in the "Name" field — nothing.
Not painted over with correction fluid. Not cut out with a scalpel, like in Camden. Just an empty field, a smooth, unfilled rectangle twenty characters long. As if whoever filled out the ledger had deliberately skipped that field. Or as if there had never been a name on that line at all — which was physically impossible, since a signature for the wages was right there.
Helen set her pencil down on the table.
Paper couldn't forget a name. It doesn't erase itself. If a name wasn't written in, then it hadn't been written in on purpose. If a signature exists but the name doesn't — then someone had made an effort to remove precisely that one fragment of information, without touching anything else.
Just — emptiness.
For the first time in all of this, Helen felt real, unexplainable fear. Not of the people erasing databases. Not of the fact that unfamiliar memories had turned up in her own head. But of this neat, clean rectangle. Because it said one thing: whatever was happening to them hadn't started yesterday. It had been laid down earlier — patiently, methodically, without hurry. By the hands of living people who knew exactly what they were doing.
She picked up her pencil and drew a light line along the empty field — not a word, not a letter, just a mark: empty here on purpose. The pressure was light, almost automatic. Exactly the kind of pressure made by someone in the habit of leaving marks on things — not for others, but for themselves. Like a scratch made with a needle on a plastic lid.
She went still.
She picked up the phone.
"The battery compartment on the camera," she said when I picked up. "Is it closed?"

title: Chapter 14
body:
I froze on the bench, without standing up.
"Yes. Closed. How do you—"
"Is there anything under the cover?"
I turned the camera over. The same roughness under my fingers — the M.L. initials, and something else I hadn't noticed yesterday in the dim room. I held the camera up to the light. A thin strip of clear tape ran along the edge of the battery cover — almost invisible, slightly yellowed with age. Someone had sealed the cover carefully from the inside. And in the middle of that strip, where the tape had been pressed onto the plastic, there was a tiny, barely visible bump. A fingertip. Someone's print, pressed down with effort, as if they wanted to be sure the tape had stuck for good.
"How did you know?" I asked quietly.
"I just drew a line in the ledger," she said. "Automatically. With the same pressure people use to scratch marks onto things so they can find them later. And I suddenly understood: whoever left those initials on the camera wasn't just marking property. He was pointing at where to look. Disposable Kodaks only have one hidden space. The battery compartment."
I pried the cover open with a fingernail. The tape split with a quiet, dry crack. There was no battery — the camera had been bought without one, the flash had never worked. Inside the little plastic rectangle of the compartment lay something folded into quarters.
I pulled it out with two fingers.
A small rectangle of photo paper, folded twice over. Thick, glossy. I unfolded it carefully, afraid of tearing it. On my palm lay a piece of photo paper roughly eight by ten centimeters.
Completely white. Utterly blank. Not a single image, not a single mark.
"There's paper here," I said. "Photo paper. But it's blank. Empty."
"Don't throw it away," Helen said without a pause, in the voice of someone who already knew the next step. "I'll be there in forty minutes."
We met in a small café that smelled of scorched milk and cheap fryer oil, tucked into the maze of alleys near Victoria Station. It always had that saving, chaotic noise — the clatter of the coffee machine, the rustle of newspapers, the footsteps of people with heavy suitcases rushing for commuter trains. Places like this are the easiest to disappear into if you're no longer in any database. Here you're just part of the transit flow. No one.
Helen was already waiting for me at a corner table by a window darkened with damp. In front of her lay that same grey folder she'd carried through the door of my office the night this whole thing started. The folder's corners had grown frayed — and that small, thoroughly mundane change somehow struck me harder than anything else that had happened these past days. We'd worn ourselves down along with that folder.
She didn't say hello. The first thing she did was hold out her hand.
"Give me the paper."
I set the white rectangle on the table in front of her. Helen looked at it for a few seconds without touching it. Then she picked it up by the very edge with two fingers and slowly brought it toward the ceramic cup of coffee the waiter had set down before I arrived. Steam rose off the coffee in a thick, steady stream.
She held the paper horizontally over the cup, a few centimeters above the surface. Silent. Still.
I watched and said nothing.
Twenty seconds passed. Thirty. And then something started happening on the white surface of the sheet that took my breath away.
Letters emerged slowly, the way an image develops in a tray of chemical solution. First barely visible, almost ghostly outlines — then darker, sharper, more certain. Not printed type. Handwriting. The same uneven, slightly left-leaning hand I'd already seen on the plastic of the camera.
Two words.
DON'T DEVELOP.
I stared at them for a long time. Helen set the paper down on the table and pushed the cup aside. The café's usual noise kept rattling on around us, but between the two of us a thick, ringing silence had formed.
"Thermochromic ink," I said quietly at last. The engineer's brain in me had gone looking for a rational explanation and found one immediately, almost with relief. "Shows up with heat. Fades again when it cools."
"Yes," Helen nodded. "A simple, reliable way to hide a message so a random person wouldn't see it. You have to know what to look for. And know how to bring it out."
"It's my handwriting," I said.
"I know."
I watched the two words slowly fading as the paper cooled, trying to work out exactly what I was feeling. Not fear. Something else — colder, quieter.
Five years ago I'd shot those twenty-four frames. Written this message. Hidden it inside the camera. Sealed it with tape. Left a fingerprint as confirmation. Given the camera to Harris — the one person I could still trust — and asked him to hide it somewhere no one would look.
The Michael from back then hadn't forgotten about this camera. He'd deliberately made sure the current Michael wouldn't develop it. But he'd also made sure the current Michael would find it.
"Did you find something?" I nodded at the folder in front of her.
She nodded, slowly, wearily:
"See for yourself."
I opened the folder. Inside were photocopies of government payroll ledgers for Harris & Croft. Neat pencil notes in the margins, in Helen's hand. Connection diagrams. And one sheet completely marked up in yellow highlighter.
"This line," her finger pointed at item forty-seven.
The same empty, clean rectangle, twenty characters long, where the name should be. But underneath this sheet lay another ledger — for the following month. And another. And another. Four months running. Every document repeated the exact same anomaly with mechanical precision. The same employee number. The same signature in the field for receiving funds.
And — absolute emptiness where the name should be.
"That's impossible," I shook my head. "Auditors would have kicked back a ledger like that on day one. The system won't process a transaction on a blank line. If a name's wiped from the database, the employee number should auto-cancel."
"That's exactly it. It wasn't erased from the database after the fact."
I picked up the pencil off the table without thinking and drew a light line, connecting the four empty fields across the different sheets. And it was only then, as my eyes focused on the signatures, that I noticed a detail that took my breath away.
All four signatures on the ledgers were identical.
Not just similar. Absolutely identical. Every line, every slant, every microscopic flourish at the end of the stroke matched to a fraction of a millimeter. I laid one transparent photocopy over the other — the outlines merged perfectly, without the slightest gap.
No living person can sign their name exactly the same way four months in a row.
I looked up. Helen was already watching me — directly, heavily, unblinking. She'd understood it before I had.
"That's not a signature," I said quietly, and my own voice sounded foreign to me in the noise of the station café. "It's an imprint. A stamp. Or a digital duplicate, laid onto the paper by a high-resolution printer."
"Yes," she breathed out. "No person was in the room when these documents were filled out. But something was simulating a physical presence. Someone had spent a very long time, very carefully, building the appearance that this empty line was… alive."
We fell silent. An elderly waiter in a dirty apron silently set two thick ceramic cups of black coffee in front of us. Life kept going on around us: a young couple laughed loudly at the next table, the barista behind the counter switched on the grinder with a deafening screech, and beyond the fogged glass of the window a huge red bus braked with a heavy sigh.
I put the photocopies back in the folder. It was exactly in that pause, in that second between one thought and the next, that the phone in my jacket pocket buzzed briefly.
It wasn't a call. Just an ordinary, standard push notification from the government authorization system — the kind that usually appear and immediately vanish from memory because they're boring and bureaucratic.
A small white rectangle glowed on the lock screen.
"Your digital identity certificate has been successfully updated."
I frowned. I hadn't updated anything. My computer was off, and my phone had lain dead as a brick in my coat pocket all night.
I unlocked the phone and opened the notification. Inside the system window were just two lines of text, in the standard font:
Update complete. Thank you, Daniel.
I stared at those six letters — D-A-N-I-E-L — and felt everything inside me drop away into emptiness with a rushing sound. Daniel Mercer. The same man whose name was now on my contract.
Helen instantly noticed how my face had changed. Her fingers gripped the edge of the table convulsively.
"What is it, Michael?"
Without a word, I turned the phone screen toward her and slid it across the lacquered wood of the table.
She read it in a second. Her pupils widened. But she didn't panic and look around. Instead, very slowly, very carefully, she set the phone back down on the table and looked — not at me. She looked at my faint, blurred reflection in the black glossy glass of the phone's dark screen. As if she needed to make sure I was still there.
"Michael," her voice dropped to a barely audible whisper.
"What?"
"They've stopped erasing you."
I didn't understand what she meant right away.
"What do you mean, stopped?"
"They're not deleting you from the system anymore, Lawson," Helen raised her eyes to me, and deep in them I saw clean, conscious dread — not panic, not confusion, but that particular, sober horror that comes at the moment you understand something irreversible. "Your ID, your tax accounts, your company, your digital signature… all of it is staying in the registries. They've simply started replacing you with someone else. Your shell is being filled in with another person, right now."
At the next table, the couple burst into cheerful laughter again. Another downpour started up outside. The barista began whistling something upbeat, wiping down glasses.
London went on living.
And I sat in the dim corner of a cheap café, understanding for the first time, really, in my skin: disappearing from this world was nowhere near the worst thing that could happen to you.
Far worse was sitting at a station one afternoon, drinking coffee gone cold, and discovering that some stranger you'd never seen was, right now, very carefully, very methodically, and entirely legally, starting to wear out the rest of your own life for you.

title: Chapter 15
body:
We left the café almost at the same moment, but walked in silence.
Sometimes a conversation ends not because the subject is exhausted. But because any new word would only tighten the noose further. The reality around us was losing its solidity, thinning out like old film stock under too powerful a projector lamp, and we both felt it.
The rain started again. Fine, suspended in the air, purely London rain. That kind of rain won't soak you through in a minute — it works differently. It settles on your eyelashes, on your jacket collar, in your hair, as a tiny cold dust, simply reminding you that you're still here. Physically. For now.
We turned toward St James's Park, hoping to lose ourselves among the scattered passersby. Halfway down the path, Helen suddenly stopped short.
"What?" I slowed, studying her frozen face.
She wasn't looking at me. Her eyes were fixed on a distant bench by a sprawling willow. A man sat there. Perfectly unremarkable — the kind of face that fades from memory before he's even out of sight around the corner. Dark jacket, a morning paper in his hands, a cardboard cup of cooling coffee. After sitting like that for a few more seconds, the man calmly stood, tucked the paper under his arm, and walked off unhurriedly toward the Mall.
"Do you know him?" I asked quietly.
Helen shook her head slowly, almost mechanically.
"No."
She paused for a long moment, watching his back — following him with her eyes to where the grey haze between the trees was already starting to swallow him up.
"But this is the third time today, Michael."
"Third what?"
"In the last four hours I've seen the same man on our route. First at Victoria, then by the tobacco shop, now here."
I spun around. The path behind us was nearly empty. The man in the dark jacket had already dissolved into the grey haze, as if he'd never been there.
"Maybe it was just nerves? Seeing things?"
"Maybe," she said too quickly. The way people speak when they don't want to pursue a subject, because the right answer is more frightening than paranoia.
Twenty minutes later we found ourselves in front of an old four-story building on the edge of Westminster. No glossy glass, no abandonment. Just an ordinary, shabby grey brick office block. Five years ago, according to the archive ledgers, this was where the accounting firm Harris & Croft had been housed.
The world had digested this place by now and moved on. On the ground floor, a private dental practice's sign gleamed; on the second, clerks from some small insurance company bustled about. And on the third, right on the fly-specked glass of the entrance, hung an old plastic sign: "OFFICES TO LET."
Nothing special. And it was exactly that perfect, mundane continuity I didn't like. If whoever was running the cleanup wanted to destroy physical traces, they'd have torched this building or bought it up whole. But here everything had been left untouched. Ordinary, cluttered life turned out to be the best camouflage for emptiness.
An elderly caretaker in a worn tweed jacket, smelling of cheap tobacco, fussed with his keys for an unbelievably long time. He apologized, wiped his glasses, complained about the old loose locks that hadn't been changed since the coronation.
While we waited in the narrow corridor, I studied the wall by the lift. Its entire surface was covered in dozens of tiny marks left by old corporate signs. Every company that had ever come through here had screwed in its brass or plastic letters, and then moved out into oblivion. All that was left were four little holes in the plaster and rectangles of slightly cleaner paint. The building's real history, written without a single word — just holes and lighter patches.
"There, please," the caretaker finally got the lock under control and pushed the heavy oak door open. "Not too long, though, I've got a plumber downstairs."
The space was completely empty. Bare white walls with faded outlines from calendars long torn down, an even layer of grey dust on the windowsills, the sharp, stale smell of old wiring and dry cardboard. Helen went straight to the window, looking out at the street through the curtain of rain. I started methodically going through the rooms, checking the empty built-in cupboards.
An ordinary, dead office. Nothing.
A couple of minutes later I'd already turned to leave when my eyes caught a strange optical inconsistency on the floor. In the far corner of what had once been reception, the carpet differed almost imperceptibly in color. An even square, roughly two meters by two. The fabric here was a shade lighter, cleaner than the rest of the surface, but the pile had been crushed down with tremendous force. I crouched and ran my palm over the stiff fibers. There were no marks from furniture legs. The weight had been distributed evenly across the whole area. As if something monolithic and unbelievably heavy had stood there, motionless, for years — something with no sharp edges, just a dense, uniform mass.
"Helen," I called.
She was beside me instantly, standing at my back. We both stared silently at that flattened square.
"A server room?" I guessed. "A rack of UPS units?"
She shook her head, scanning the ceiling and corners:
"No. There's no forced ventilation for a server room here. And no power cabling runs to this corner either."
I ran my palm over the carpet again, moving toward the join with the skirting board, and my fingers found something small and cold. A tiny metal plate right against the wall, no bigger than a fingernail. No markings. Just a matte scrap of gun-metal steel, set flush with the floor.
I took my keys out of my pocket and carefully levered the plate up with an edge. It gave way with a click and lifted. Underneath was an old cable channel sunk into the concrete. Empty. Completely dry and clean — as if someone had been maintaining it, not letting dust collect.
Except for one single object.
At the bottom of the narrow plastic channel lay an ordinary sheet of white A4 paper, folded neatly in half. I pulled it out with two fingers. No trace of age-old dust — the sheet was fresh, as if it had been placed here if not today, then certainly this week.
I unfolded it. On the first side, dead center, sat a single line, printed on an old laser printer with the characteristic faint grain of dried toner:
If you're reading this, then we're too late again.
I heard Helen behind me draw a sharp, hissing breath.
I flipped the page over, hands unsteady. Completely blank. The back of it too. No signatures, no dates. Just those eight words.
And in that moment I understood clearly what frightened me most about this discovery.
This message wasn't addressed to me. It wasn't addressed to any specific person at all. Whoever had left this sheet under the raised floor of an office long gone hadn't been calculating our exact steps. They were simply following an iron mathematical logic: in this system, sooner or later, someone would come here anyway. And that someone would make exactly the same mistakes.

title: Chapter 16
body:
For a few more seconds we stared silently at the white sheet of paper.
Then I carefully folded it back in half, trying to match the old creases exactly. For some reason it felt wrong to keep it unfolded. Every object in this world has a natural, safe state. This letter preferred to stay closed.
"Do we take it?" I asked.
Helen nodded, brief and decisive.
I was already slipping the folded sheet into her grey folder when the caretaker appeared cautiously in the doorway. He shifted his weight from foot to foot, the keys jingling softly in his hand.
"Sorry… Did you find anything? Any old documents?"
I shook my head automatically:
"No. Nothing."
"Shame," the old man said with complete sincerity. There wasn't a trace of professional curiosity in his voice. An ordinary London pensioner who just wanted to be useful. He'd already turned to leave, but paused right at the threshold. "Though…"
Helen and I reacted at the same instant — turning our heads in sync.
"Though what?" I asked quickly.
The caretaker frowned, rubbing his unshaven chin in a funny way.
"About two weeks ago… yes, that's right, last Tuesday. A man came round here too. Asking specifically about this office on the third floor."
Behind me, Helen straightened slowly, taut as a wire.
"Did he look like us? From a ministry?" she asked.
"No… not at all," the caretaker thought about it. "More like… tired. Very tired, you understand? You looked at him and it seemed like the man hadn't slept in weeks. Bags under his eyes, a heavy look. Said he was assessing the property. His papers were all in order, official forms, everything proper. Paid cash. Very polite. Looked the place over for ten minutes, no more. And left."
"Was he looking for something?" I asked. "Checking the walls?"
"I suppose… actually, no," the old man shook his head. "He acted a bit strange. Like he hadn't come to search, just to confirm that nothing was left here anymore. Stood in the middle of the room, looked around the corners, sighed heavily — and that was it."
A dense, muffled silence settled over the empty office. Through the window came the hiss of tires on wet asphalt.
"Do you remember his face?" Helen took a step toward the old man.
He smiled, apologetic, bewildered:
"Funny thing… not really, now. I remember the voice — quiet, a bit hoarse. I remember the coat — dark, expensive, but badly worn. I remember he kept coughing into a handkerchief. But the face… no. Nothing at all. I try to remember, and it's like it's been cut off. A grey smudge."
We already knew that symptom.
When the caretaker went back down to the ground floor to his plumber, giving us five more minutes, we started going over the room again. Not like investigators hunting for clues, but like people trying to reconstruct the logic of someone else's movements. Someone who'd been here before us.
I went back to the lighter square on the carpet. Knelt down on one knee, put my face almost to the floor, catching the sidelong light from the window.
And that's when a cold sweat broke over me. The compression marks in the carpet were too deep. Too solid. Whatever this object was, it hadn't stood here for one year. Or five. The backing had practically fused into the concrete beneath it, and the carpet fibers had lost every trace of spring, permanently remembering some colossal foreign weight.
"Helen," I called, without getting up off my knee.
She came over silently. I pointed to the edge of the flattened square:
"See the pattern?"
She studied it closely for a long time, head tilted slightly. The light from the window fell sideways, and in that slanted glow the crushed fibers cast tiny shadows, making the square stand out clearly, almost like a footprint in snow.
"It's not furniture," I said. "Furniture doesn't weigh this much, and no one keeps a piece in the middle of an empty reception for decades."
"No. Not furniture."
Helen walked slowly to the panoramic window. Looked down into the internal light well, where the bins sat soaking in the rain, then turned back to the empty room.
"Michael…" her voice came out flat, as if she were speaking words she hadn't fully grasped herself yet. "Do you know what's directly below us?"
"The dentist and the insurance office. We saw the signs."
"Not in the building," she pulled the phone from her pocket. Without turning on mobile data, Helen opened an offline photo of the building's cross-section plans — one she'd taken of the fire-evacuation board by the lift. For a few seconds her finger traced slowly over the faded construction lines. Then it stopped. And she silently turned the screen toward me.
The spot of our light-colored square on the plan matched the axis lines of the load-bearing structure exactly, down to the millimeter. But below it, on the lower floors, there were no rooms. No service niches, no ventilation shafts, no basement. On the architectural drawing, under this exact section of the third floor, there was just one terse word written into an empty rectangle:
VOID
A void. A sealed shaft running clean through the whole building from foundation to roof, boxed in by solid concrete walls.
"A planning consultant's error? A construction defect?"
"Maybe," Helen answered. But her tone made it clear she'd stopped believing in that saving explanation a while ago.
We switched off the dim overhead light and stepped out into the corridor. When the heavy lock of the entrance door clicked shut with a dull metallic sound, I turned automatically and looked through the narrow glass pane into the dark office.
There, deep in the empty room, for a split second I could have sworn someone was standing. A tall, motionless grey figure. Right in the center of that same light-colored square. Watching us through the dark.
I stopped short. Blinked.
The room was completely empty. Only grey glints of streetlight trembled on the bare walls.
"What is it, Michael?" Helen touched my sleeve gently.
I stared into the glass rectangle for a few more seconds. Then slowly shook my head:
"Nothing. I imagined it. My mind's slipping."
But all the way down the stairs, a suffocating feeling wouldn't leave me: today, we hadn't been the first ones in that empty office. Not even the second. Someone invisible was standing there right now, listening to our footsteps fade away down the stairwell.

title: Chapter 17
body:
We'd almost reached the glass pavilions of Westminster station when the phone came alive in my jacket pocket.
A dry, sharp buzz. On the screen glowed an empty grey line — "Number withheld." My finger was already hovering over the red icon, about to decline, when Helen caught my arm. Her cold fingers closed tightly around my wrist, her eyes ordering:
"Answer it."
I let out a breath and pressed the phone to my ear.
"Lawson."
For a few seconds, absolute silence reigned on the other end. Then heavy, rasping breath reached me. And a man's voice — very quiet, flat, stripped of any intonation, as if the man were spending enormous effort just pushing air through his vocal cords:
"Are you still looking for Thomas Harris?"
I froze in the middle of the pavement. Helen stopped the same instant. She couldn't hear the words coming through the speaker, but she understood everything from my face — from how my jaw instantly turned to stone.
"Who's speaking?" I tried to make my voice as level as possible.
A pause. Long, viscous.
"That makes absolutely no difference right now, Michael."
He'd used my first name. Not "Mr. Lawson," not "sir" — just Michael. The way you address people you've known a long time. People you knew before they forgot themselves.
"Where did you get this number?" I stepped back, pressing against a brick wall. "It's not in any active City database."
A short, dry sound came from the other end of the line. Something like a laugh. Very tired, and bitter.
"Michael… if I'd wanted to, I could have called you on this exact number five years ago. On the very day you first walked through the door of the office in Kensington."
Everything inside me frosted over at once. This man knew me. Had known the trajectory of my life long before this entire nightmare broke loose. Not from a database — from memory. Living, unrewritten memory.
"What do you want?"
"From you? Nothing. I've stayed silent too long. Watched reality melt for too long. Now, I think, it's my turn to talk."
I shifted my grip on the phone, catching Helen's eye.
"Is Harris alive?" I asked, point blank.
The breathing on the line broke off for a second, growing even heavier. Then — a strained cough, short, suppressed. The very cough into a handkerchief the caretaker had just mentioned. I was hearing it for the second time today. The first time — from his mouth, retold in someone else's words. Now — directly, down the line, in my ear.
Something inside me began to turn, slowly, with a grinding creak.
"Yes," the voice answered at last.
I closed my eyes. For the past weeks, Helen and I had been operating on a single axiom: Thomas Harris had vanished, been scrubbed from the registries, and therefore was physically gone. And now that entire carefully built chain of logic collapsed on a single short, hoarse word.
"Where is he?" I asked quickly. "If he's alive, where do I find him?"
The answer came without hesitation:
"I don't know."
"What do you mean, you don't know? You just said—"
"Exactly what I said, Michael." For a second, something entered the voice that I couldn't identify right away. Not tiredness. Something deeper — like the pain of a man used to speaking precisely, now forced to speak this way because it's the only thing that remains true. "Thomas Harris is alive. His heart is physically beating, he walks these streets. But I no longer know which of the people I meet in the crowd every day is actually him."
I felt icy dread run down my spine. This was beyond comprehension.
"Explain. What does that mean?"
"I can't," the voice cut him off. "If I explain it to you now, you'll simply stop. Give up and quit looking. And you need to keep looking. All the way to the end."
"Then why did you even call?!" My composure cracked, and I dropped into a low growl. "What's the point of this conspiracy-theory routine?"
A long, suffocating pause stretched out. I could hear the man on the other end cough hard again — and suppress it the way you suppress something shameful you don't want anyone to see. And then he spoke a line that settled in my head like a dead weight, driving out every other thought:
"Because right now, you're repeating my own mistakes, step for step."
A pause. One second.
"And I couldn't stay silent a second time."
There was a short click on the line. The connection died.
We stood motionless under the wide concrete overhang of the tube station for another ten minutes or so. The rain behind us picked up with new force, turning the London evening into one solid grey wall. Streams of water rushed noisily over the asphalt, people hurried past us with their faces hidden under umbrellas. But Helen and I stayed fixed points in this landscape that no longer belonged to us — as if the two of us had, at the same moment, run out of the ability to move at the same pace as everything around us.
I told her the whole conversation. Almost word for word, trying to keep even the intonations and pauses of that hoarse, exhausted voice. Helen listened in silence, without interrupting, only her fingers tightening further around the strap of her bag.
When I finished, she studied my eyes for a long time. Then she asked only one thing:
"What scared you the most, out of all of it?"
I didn't answer right away. Took out a cigarette, tried to light it, but the lighter had gotten damp, so I just turned the little roll of tobacco between my fingers, then threw it in a bin.
"Not that Harris is alive," I said quietly. "Not even that this man knows my personal number and remembers me from five years back. What frightened me to the bone was the ending. His last line."
"'You're repeating my mistakes'?"
"No. The last one."
Helen frowned slightly.
"'I couldn't stay silent a second time,'" I repeated. "You hear it? A second time. He stayed silent the first time. Five years ago. When he could still have changed something."
Helen was quiet for a long time, watching raindrops shatter against the granite curb, scattering into tiny drops that vanished instantly, as if they'd never existed. Then, almost in a whisper, barely audible over the roar of a passing train, she said:
"So… there was already an investigation, before us. Someone found this exact camera, the same way. Went to the photo lab in Camden, the same way. Stood in that empty office on the third floor and looked at the flattened square of carpet, the same way."
We turned and looked at each other at the same instant. For the first time in this whole chase — not as people bound together by shared trouble. But as two people who'd suddenly understood, with clean, mathematical clarity: we weren't the first ones through here. We were simply walking in someone else's deep footprints, through thick fog.
And the most terrifying part was that those footprints might not end somewhere up ahead, at a point of triumphant revelation.
They'd already broken off, long ago. Right where we were standing.

title: Chapter 18
body:
Who wanted us to find that letter?
Up until that moment, as we went down into the stuffy, damp-iron-smelling mouth of the tube station, I'd only been asking myself one question: who wrote it? But now, with the echo of the phone call still ringing in my ears, the question mutated. For the first time, a truly chilling thought cut through.
What if that letter hadn't been written for us at all?
We didn't go down to the platform. Instead we squeezed into the corner of a cramped Turkish takeaway drenched in sickly fluorescent light, right by the entrance to the underground. People were bustling around us, the air thick with the smell of overused fryer oil and cheap spices, but for us all that noise had turned into a dull background hum. Once again, we laid the white A4 sheet, pulled from under the floor of the abandoned office, out on the sticky plastic of the table.
I wasn't reading the line. I was looking at the physical medium itself. And right there, under the merciless neon lights, the engineer's pedantry finally took over.
The paper was too white. Too fresh. It didn't have that faint yellowing or greying that any pulp inevitably picks up after five years sitting in a sealed cable channel. It didn't smell of stale damp. A standard 80-gram office sheet, manufactured at most a few months ago. It had been placed under that carpet very recently.
The caretaker's words surfaced in my head immediately: "About two weeks ago, a man came round here too… Very tired… Looked the place over for ten minutes and left."
The whole picture flipped upside down.
That man, two weeks ago, hadn't come to the empty office to look for traces. He'd come to leave one. Lifted the metal plate, dropped the folded sheet into the empty cable channel, and snapped the cover shut.
This completely changed the direction of the investigation. The question of who was erasing people fell to second place. Now a different, far more dangerous figure stepped onto the stage.
Who was trying to leave traces before they were destroyed for good?
"He's helping us, Michael," Helen argued with me for the first time in a long while, her voice ringing with a dull, desperate stubbornness. "This man is ahead of us. He's leaving markers so we don't go blind."
"No," I cut in sharply, pushing away my untouched cup of tea. "He's not helping. Look closer. Every single time, he ends up at the right point one step ahead of us. And every single time, he leaves exactly enough information for us to take one, precisely defined next step. Not more, not less. It's a measured dose. If he genuinely wanted to lay his cards on the table, he'd have written everything. Addresses, names, passwords. Instead he leaves one line. Why?"
I reached into the grey folder and pulled out every note we'd gathered over these days. Laid them out in a row on the sticky table, like cards in a game of patience.
Check the bottom of the suitcase.
↓
You're looking for the wrong man.
↓
If you're reading this, then we're too late again.
None of these lines explained anything. They gave no answers. They simply steered our route. We were being led down a corridor, crumbs dropped for us with elegant precision.
And that's when I noticed the thing that finally stripped away my illusions. As a programmer, I was used to working with patterns and system micro-defects. I brought my face close to the three sheets. In all three, the font was identical — standard Courier New. But it wasn't about the typeface. On all three sheets, the letter 'e' had a tiny, barely visible white speck in the upper loop — a toner-fusing defect on a laser printer's drum. And a faint, almost invisible vertical streak along the right edge — wear from a worn cartridge.
One printer. One cartridge. One grain.
"He's not leaving clues, Helen," I said, and my voice came out frighteningly calm. "He's writing a manual."
Helen was silent for a long time, looking at the three sheets. For a second, the noise of the takeaway around us seemed to fall away.
"Then…" she raised her darkened eyes to me. "This manual isn't addressed to us. Whoever writes it just knows this chain of events will inevitably bring someone here. To him, we're just the ones executing the algorithm."
She said it as if she weren't afraid. As if she'd already grown used to the fact that the most terrifying things don't shout — they arrive quietly and sit down beside you.
22:45
I went home alone. Helen stayed in Westminster — she needed to try to cross-reference the employee number from the ledger against other sealed archives.
I went up to my floor, my legs leaden with exhaustion. Took out my keys, turned the lock. The door gave way quietly, opening onto a dark hallway smelling of stale coffee.
I dropped my keys onto the side table with a jingle, and was already reaching for the light switch when my eyes caught a white shape on the floor. A heavy envelope lay right at the gap under the front door.
No stamp. No recipient's address. Not a single signature or postmark. It had simply been pushed through into the flat by hand while I was out.
I picked it up. The envelope was cold. I carefully tore open the edge and shook the contents out onto my palm.
There were no documents. No diagrams, no notes, no printouts with tell-tale printer defects. An ordinary glossy photograph, ten by fifteen centimeters, slid onto my palm. A physical, analog print.
I switched on the hallway light. The yellow beam struck the gloss.
The photograph was of me.
Five years ago. I was wearing an old jacket I'd thrown out the winter before last, and the very same watch ticking on my wrist right now. I was standing on the front steps of the grey brick Harris & Croft building in Westminster. Looking straight into the camera lens — open, confident. And smiling. It was the smile of a man who has everything in order, who knows exactly where he is and what he's doing.
But that wasn't the most frightening part.
To my right, his hand resting on my shoulder in a friendly way, stood a man. In his early fifties, tall, in a good suit. Dark hair greying at the temples. Straight posture. The face of a man used to being listened to. We stood side by side, like old acquaintances, like people who shared a common cause.
I didn't know this man.
I looked at him for a long time. Then again. Tried to latch onto anything at all — the shape of his face, a gesture, something in how he held himself. Nothing. A completely unfamiliar man, in a photograph where he stood beside me with his arm around my shoulder.
Someone had circled his face in red marker — thick, careful, almost ceremonial.
Until that night, everything happening had felt like an external threat. Something that erased files, forged signatures in ledgers, changed names in databases — out there, external, not touching me directly. But looking at that glossy piece of paper, I truly understood for the first time: whatever was happening to us wasn't working on computers. It was working on me. On my own memory. On the one thing I'd believed I could still trust.
Five years ago I'd stood next to this man. His hand on my shoulder, he'd looked into the lens right along with me. And I'd smiled. And now his face was as unfamiliar to me as the face of a random passerby outside my window.

title: Chapter 19
body:
The photograph on my table wasn't evidence in the usual sense. Evidence points to a culprit, connects facts, builds logic. This piece of glossy paper did the opposite — it was breaking into me from the inside.
I sat under the lamp almost all night, studying the print. But I wasn't looking at the unfamiliar man in the red circle. I was looking at myself.
The man in the photo felt like a stranger to me, a double who'd stolen my name. I dug into the mundane details with my eyes, trying to grab hold of anything tangible. There were the old scratched-glass watch — still ticking on my wrist right now. There was the jacket, its left sleeve still showing a tiny cigarette-ember burn hole, scorched in some pub I also didn't remember. Old trainers with a dirty white sole. The posture — slightly turned, relaxed. And the smile.
I stared into that smile until my eyes started to water. It wasn't the reflexive grimace people give for a random snapshot. My eyes in the photo weren't fixed on empty space. They were alive, warm. I was looking at the person holding the camera. I was smiling at him.
07:15
I called Helen the moment the grey London morning began seeping through the blinds. She picked up on the first ring, as if she hadn't slept at all.
"Helen, I know what's missing from that photograph."
"What?" her voice came out hoarse on the line, compressed with exhaustion.
"The photographer."
Forty minutes later she was at my place. We spread the photograph out on the kitchen table, right under the pale morning light coming through the window. We stopped analyzing faces. We started analyzing the geometry of the shot. The direction of the shadows. The angle of the sunlight. The reflections in the window glass of the Harris & Croft building behind us.
And it was there, in the reflection of the heavy glass entrance door, that we found something strange.
The sun stood high, behind the photographer's back, and the glass surface of the door worked like an imperfect, dark mirror. In that reflection you could clearly make out the silhouette of a person with a camera raised to their face. You could see an elbow bent, a solid shoulder, the outline of a jacket. Where the head should have been, the glass stayed blurred — too much backlight.
"A developing defect?" I asked, feeling a familiar dull nausea start building inside me.
Helen shook her head slowly.
"No. Look closer at how he's holding his hands."
I took an old magnifying glass out of a drawer. No digital zoom — just a piece of curved glass, bringing the grain of the photo paper closer.
I trained the loupe on the dark reflection of the photographer's hands. The grain blurred, but the outline of the object in his fingers became obvious. The person wasn't holding a heavy DSLR up to their face, or a compact digital camera. It was the distinctive, boxy shape of cheap plastic. The characteristic bump of a flash unit. A yellow-green rim on the plastic housing.
A disposable Kodak. That exact one.
Helen silently reached into her bag, took out the very disposable camera we'd found in the hiding place, and set it carefully on the table, right beside the glossy print.
On the bottom edge of the plastic body, right by the battery cover, a deep, uneven scratch showed dark — the mark left by someone once forcing it open with a knife or a screwdriver. A distinctive, jagged gouge, impossible to mistake for a factory defect or accidental wear.
I picked up the loupe again and pointed it at the reflection in the glass door in the photograph. Right where the photographer's fingers gripped the bottom of the plastic body, the dark glass of the door showed exactly the same tiny, jagged white mark.
The scratch matched down to the millimeter.
We both fell silent.
"Harris," I said quietly. Not a question — a statement of fact. "He's the one holding the camera. He took this photo."
Helen raised her eyes to me. She'd already understood.
"He took the camera from you. That exact day. The last photograph before everything ended. You gave him the camera, stood next to him," she paused. "And smiled."
The air in the kitchen turned as thick as cement. I looked at my own smiling face in the photograph and understood one simple, devastating thing. I remembered absolutely nothing — a complete, ringing blank — about this man standing beside me. Didn't remember his hand on my shoulder. Didn't remember him raising the camera and looking through the viewfinder.
I didn't remember that day at all.
And that's when, for the first time in all these weeks, rage woke up in me. Real, hot, human anger. Not at the erased databases. At myself.
"Why don't I remember anything?!" I snapped, and my own voice sounded foreign to me in the quiet kitchen. "What the hell was I standing there for, smiling, shaking his hand, if all of it's been erased?! Who gave anyone the right to cut pieces out of my own head?!"
I slammed my fist down on the table. The cups rattled, and the light, glossy photograph jumped from the impact, flipped into the air, and landed back on the table's plastic surface.
Face down.
I went still, breathing hard, staring at the greyish back of the photo paper.
There were no Kodak factory stamps. No date. Right in the center of the sheet, slightly at an angle, two words showed dark. They'd been written in ballpoint pen — broad strokes, with a distinctive heavy pressure and a particular, angular slant to the letters.
It was my own handwriting.
DON'T DEVELOP.

title: Chapter 20
body:
I stared at those two words until the letters lost their meaning and turned into an abstract tangle of ink lines.
If someone else had left that line, I wouldn't have hesitated a second. Any warning from another person in an investigation like this is just a marker of fear, someone else's version of the truth. But my own hand had made these letters. I knew the anatomy of my own handwriting too well to look for shelter in self-deception. Heavy pressure, pressing into the paper. The nearly vertical stroke of the letter D. The disproportionately long crossbar of the T. I only wrote like that in two situations: when I was in a mad hurry, and when I was absolutely, rock-solid certain of what I was doing.
Five years ago I'd left myself a direct, unambiguous message.
And now, for the first time in this whole investigation, I faced not a technical problem but a deeply intuitive one: should I trust the man I used to be? Did that past Michael Lawson have any right to dictate terms to the one I was now?
Helen and I barely spoke. She made coffee in silence, set a heavy earthenware mug down in front of me, and sat across from me, legs tucked underneath her. The yellow plastic of the disposable Kodak lay right in the middle of the table. Neither of us touched it. The camera no longer looked like a piece of evidence or a key to the mystery. More like an unexploded shell that would detonate at the slightest careless movement.
"You still want to develop it, don't you?" Helen asked quietly, watching my face over the rim of her cup.
