I was quiet for a long time, listening to some car engine turning over lazily outside the window. Then, to my own surprise, I said:
"No."
"No?"
"Not yet."
"Why, Michael? The answers to everything are in there."
Carefully, trying not to smudge the old ink, I turned the photograph face-up again. Two figures looked back at us: a smiling, thriving Michael, and the unfamiliar man in the red circle.
"Because the man in this photograph knows an order of magnitude more about what's happening than I do today. Imagine, Helen, that five years ago I had to choose between two opposite options. Develop this film and set off an avalanche. Or lock it away in the dark forever. If I chose the second option, back then, in my right mind — then I had a reason. One strong and frightening enough to write myself an order. Not a request, not advice. An order. And I don't want to break it until I understand who I was up against."
Helen looked at me for a long time. Then nodded slowly.
After breakfast, for the first time in days, I went out not to chase a lead. I went out to buy stationery.
An ordinary little shop in a residential block near Paddington. Cramped shelves of school exercise books, envelopes, cheap markers. An elderly shop assistant behind the counter lazily re-tagged price stickers with a gun that clicked, monotonous and irritating, through the whole store.
I picked out a thick notebook with a hard black cover. The plainest one, no logos, no lines or squares — just clean, thick white pages. I added an ordinary black ballpoint pen to it.
"A gift for someone?" the woman at the till smiled amiably, packing the purchase into a rustling bag.
"No," I shook my head. "For myself."
"My, that's a big one. Starting your memoirs, are you?"
I smiled grimly back at her:
"I want to get down what I still remember, while I still can."
The woman handed me my change and sighed knowingly:
"Good habit, young man. These days it's all phones, clouds… people trust everything to screens. But paper — paper's more reliable. It remembers a long time."
That casual, throwaway line hit me far harder than she could have imagined. Paper is more reliable. Paper doesn't update digital certificates. Paper doesn't change names in a database with a snap of someone's fingers.
Back at the flat, I sat down at the table, opened to the first page, and wrote a single line: "What I remember today."
Then I stopped.
It turned out this mental investigation — inside my own head — was the hardest thing I'd faced yet. I remembered my childhood in vivid detail. Remembered my first serious job, my internship, moving to London. But the moment I tried to consciously approach events from five years back, logic started to stall.
There was no black hole there. No sense of a cut-out fragment, no phantom pain. There was fog. Thick, matte, perfectly uniform fog. The memory existed — I could feel its physical presence — but someone had very carefully, with jeweler's precision, covered this one particular layer of my life with frosted glass.
I got angry and started writing down everything, without order or chronology. Names of London streets, names of old business contacts, database passwords I'd changed three years ago, random smells, favorite coffee blends, music, old phone numbers. Anything that surfaced from the bottom of my mind.
An hour and a half later I'd filled nearly twenty pages. I read them back from start to finish. And my breath caught.
In this enormous, chaotic stream of personal memories, there wasn't a single mention of the stranger from the photograph. Not a single hint of Harris & Croft. My mind had painstakingly recorded a thousand mundane details, but had completely, sterilely skipped over the man I'd stood arm in arm with in that photo. That, in itself, was already irrefutable evidence. My memory had been deliberately deformed.
Around noon, the phone on the table buzzed briefly. A text message from Helen lit up the screen:
"I checked your handwriting."
I dialed her number instantly.
"Remember those government payroll ledgers for Harris & Croft?" Her voice was drawn tight as a wire. "Four months, empty fields instead of a name."
"Of course."
"I went back and compared all the sheets again in detail, under magnification. On the very last one, for December… on that same line without a name, no digital duplicate of the signature was placed. But right next to the empty field, on the grey margin of the page, someone made a short, barely visible note in ballpoint pen."
I went still, feeling my heart give a heavy, painful thud.
"What note?"
A long pause hung on the other end of the line.
"It's in your handwriting, Michael. Your pressure. Your D."
I sank slowly back into the chair, staring at the open black notebook in front of me.
"What does it say?"
Helen answered almost in a whisper, and for the first time I heard in her voice not paranoia, but deep, genuine pity for me:
"It says: 'It's too late already.'"
I hung up without even saying goodbye. The phone dropped from my fingers onto the table.
I stared at the five-year-old photograph. Then at the plastic camera lying next to it. Then at the fresh ink in my open notebook. And for the first time in this entire insane investigation, a thought crossed my mind that had never even come close before.
What if, all these five years, no one had been trying to erase me by force — from outside, with someone else's hands? What if I myself, with my own hands, had deliberately made sure I'd never remember this past?

title: Chapter 21
body:
For the rest of the day I couldn't shake one single, nagging thought.
All this time, Helen and I had been chasing other people's ghosts. First the stranger in the red circle. Then the man in the worn dark coat, coughing into a handkerchief. Then the phantom photographer whose reflection had dissolved in a glass door. Then the author of the printed notes with the toner defect. But not once, in this entire insane investigation, had I asked myself the most obvious question.
If five years ago I'd understood the mechanics of what was happening well enough to leave myself instructions in the margins of government ledgers and on the backs of photographs — then where were the rest of the instructions? I couldn't have entrusted my life to just two random lines. There had to be something else.
I went to the shelving unit in the hallway and took down a heavy, grey-dusted archive box of thick cardboard from the top shelf. It had moved with me from flat to flat for years. I'd almost never opened it. It just sat in the corner like ballast, a silent witness to the fact that I'd once had a past, and that I hadn't wanted to part with it radically enough to throw the whole thing away.
Inside lay the most ordinary of lives, recorded on paper. Old tenancy agreements, warranty cards for appliances thrown out long ago, yellowed utility bills. A few empty notebooks still in unopened cellophane. A thick stack of business cards from people whose names meant nothing to me. Boarding passes, insurance policies, tax notices a decade old.
An hour later the whole living room was buried in paper. Helen helped in silence. I couldn't even remember when she'd arrived, or letting her in.
She sat down on the floor right in the middle of the paper chaos and methodically sorted documents by year, building neat stacks.
"Keep this?"
"Yes."
"Throw this out?"
"No."
That day, almost everything stayed exactly where it was. For the first time in my life, everyday clutter had stopped being clutter.
Toward evening, as the shadows from the windows stretched across the whole room, Helen lifted an old planner from the bottom of the box. Quite thin, in a cheap black faux-leather cover, its corners worn.
"Michael," she called softly.
"What?"
"You've never used paper planners in your life, have you? You always said a phone organizer was the only workable system."
I answered automatically, without even thinking:
"Right. Never used one."
And immediately caught myself short. My throat closed. If I'd never used them, then why was this planner sitting in my own home, at the very bottom of an archive box? So someone had used it after all. And that someone had worn my clothes, and signed with my handwriting.
I stepped over quickly, took the book from her, and opened to the first page.
January. Perfectly clean, not a single mark.
February. Also empty.
March. A few short work meetings, noted in my own cramped hand — server names, backup timings. The handwriting unmistakably mine, but the content foreign to me, like the diary of a stranger found on a park bench.
April…
I froze. The April pages had been torn out, carefully, with surgical precision. Not one page. Not two. Almost the entire month was gone from the binding — cut with a blade, right down to the spine, along the glue line, so as not to damage the rest of the binding. From the outside it looked as if April had never existed at all — just a clean jump from March straight into May, without a single seam.
"What year is this?" Helen leaned in closer.
I turned the planner over and looked at the faded gold stamping on the cover. Five years ago. That exact year. That exact month when Harris & Croft had started dissolving into thin air — in the payroll records, in the ledger signatures, in the memory of everyone who'd ever touched it.
I was about to close the planner when my fingers, gripping the back cover, felt a strange, barely detectable unevenness. The back cover was slightly thicker than the front. Just a little, a fraction of a millimeter. The fabric backing of the cover was pulled tighter than it needed to be, in one spot. Something else was underneath it. Something completely flat, rigid, with sharp rectangular edges, hidden so carefully it could only be discovered by hand — never by eye.
Helen watched my fingers in silence. Her breathing was quick and uneven.
"Are you going to open it?" she asked in a whisper.
I held the planner in my hands for a long time, feeling its strange, shifted center of gravity. The room was very quiet — just the occasional sound from the street and the quiet ticking of the wall clock, which I'd never noticed before.
Then, slowly but with absolute firmness, I shook my head.
"No."
"Why?" genuine confusion flashed in her eyes. "There could be something in there that gives you April back."
I looked at the five-year-old photograph, still lying on the dining table face-down, hiding its inked warning from the world.
"Because that photograph says 'DON'T DEVELOP.' And for the first time in my life I want to do something I've never known how to do before — trust the man I used to be. If that past Michael Lawson sewed something into this cardboard cover and buried it at the very bottom of an archive box, then he was counting on me finding it one day. But maybe the algorithm is built so that I'm not supposed to open it today. We haven't taken the right steps yet."
I carefully closed the planner and set it on the edge of the table, right on top of the glossy print.
My past lay in front of me, sealed in cardboard and glue. And for the first time I felt like I was playing chess against myself. Against an opponent who'd calculated every one of my moves five years in advance — and who, most frighteningly of all, also carried my name.
Outside the window, London slowly sank into dusk. Somewhere down on the street, a passerby coughed — short, strained, into their jacket collar. I lifted my head. Listened.
Silence.
Just the ticking of the clock. And the black notebook, open to the page where, in my own handwriting, it read: "What I remember today" — and twenty pages further down, not one single name I was supposed to know.

title: Chapter 22
body:
The most terrifying discovery rarely comes at the moment you find a new piece of evidence.
It comes later.
When you're alone. When the most ordinary things start existing around you again — a kettle, rain against the window, a cold cup of coffee. And you suddenly understand the world has already changed, even though no one noticed.
That day I didn't go anywhere else. I had no strength left.
Over the past weeks I'd gotten used to reacting the same way every time: a new find meant a new place, a new archive, a new witness. Keep moving, always. As long as you're moving, it feels like you're in control of what's happening. But now, for the first time, movement had lost its meaning.
If the person who wrote 'Don't Develop' was me… then who was I running from?
I sat down at the kitchen table.
Three things lay in front of me. The black notebook. The disposable Kodak. The photograph where Harris and I were smiling as if nothing but the most ordinary workday lay ahead of us.
I moved my eyes from one to the other. Waited for one of them to speak first.
None of them did.
An hour later, Helen arrived.
She didn't ask anything. Just took off her wet coat, set a paper bag from the nearest bakery on the table, and gave me that short, measuring look I'd already learned to recognize.
"Have you eaten?"
I shook my head.
She silently pulled out two still-warm croissants. Put the kettle on. Found mugs in the cupboard that I myself hadn't been able to locate in six months. We ate, barely talking, and outside the window darkness fell without us noticing, the way it does in late October, when night doesn't so much arrive as suddenly turn out to have been there for a while.
That's probably exactly why this late meal stuck with me sharper than dozens of archives and police corridors. Because over these past weeks, we'd stopped being two people. We'd become an investigation. And only now, sitting across from each other with hot coffee and pastry, did I suddenly notice that Helen was tired too — genuinely, not for show. Dark half-moons sat under her eyes. She kept taking her glasses off and rubbing the bridge of her nose. Sometimes, when she thought I wasn't looking, she'd just close her eyes for a few seconds. Not because she was falling asleep. Because remembering was getting heavy.
"Michael."
"What?"
"If it turns out you really did all of this yourself…" she took a long time choosing her words, and I didn't rush her. "Will you stop looking?"
I looked at the photograph.
"I don't know."
"And if it turns out the past you was right?"
That question turned out to be heavier than any that came before. Because for the first time there was no answer that could be checked on the spot.
In the evening, after Helen left, I set the old notebook aside and opened the new one — the one I'd bought yesterday at the stationery shop by the tube. The old one was too full of other people's traces, other people's questions. I needed clean space.
On the first page of the new notebook, in my own hand, already stood: "What I remember today" — I'd written it yesterday, right after buying it, just to begin. To fix the intention.
I stared at that line for a long time. Then started leafing further — slowly, page by page. The first thirty sheets were completely blank. White, untouched, with the faint smell of printer's ink.
But starting from page thirty-one, there were numbers in the top right corner.
Neat. In pencil. Handwritten.
I stopped.
I picked up a pen. Wrote the number "1" and slowly brought it beside the number "31."
The pressure. The slant. The way of writing a three — with a short, downward serif tail I'd never consciously noticed about myself before, but recognized instantly, without a doubt.
It was my handwriting. Mine. Absolutely certain.
But I didn't remember ever opening this notebook before yesterday.
The phone buzzed briefly. A message from Helen — just one line:
"Check the receipt from the shop."
I pulled out the receipt I'd stuffed into my pocket that morning without thinking.
Date. Time. Black notebook, blue pen — it all matched. Except for one line item. The very first, topmost one.
Photocopying — 31 pp.
I read the receipt again. Then again.
I hadn't made any copies. I hadn't even gone near the photocopier by the till. I'd simply taken the notebook off the shelf, paid, and left.
Very slowly, I raised my eyes to the open notebook.
Thirty blank pages. Numbering that started at thirty-one. A legitimate receipt recording an action I hadn't taken.
For the first time in this whole investigation, I felt truly afraid — not at the thought of being watched. But at the thought that there was another version of me. One that kept doing things. Acting. Paying. Copying.
And leaving behind it nothing but perfectly ordinary, unremarkable receipts.

title: Chapter 23
body:
I never thought a receipt could scare me more than a gun.
A gun is at least honest. It doesn't pretend to be part of normal life.
But a receipt is a scrap of paper you usually crumple up and toss in the first bin you pass. That's exactly why you trust it. It doesn't know how to lie. Or, more precisely, it has no reason to. It just records what happened.
All night I kept rereading one line.
Photocopying — 31 pages.
If the till had printed it, then someone really had used the photocopier. There was only one question. Who?
Helen showed up at eight in the morning, without calling ahead. She'd stopped calling ahead — that too had happened quietly, like so much else over the past weeks. At some point it had simply become obvious that no warning was needed.
"We're going there," she said, without taking off her coat.
"Where?"
"The shop."
"You think they'll remember something?"
She shrugged — brief, no wasted words.
"People rarely remember faces. But sometimes they remember something odd very well."
Outside it was damp. Not rain — just that particular London mist that never soaks your clothes but somehow, by the end of the day, has gotten into everything. We walked quickly, without talking. Helen kept her hands in the pockets of her coat — the same one she'd been wearing for four years now. I knew that, though I'd never consciously noticed it.
The stationery shop met us with the same smell of paper and cheap plastic. Behind the till stood yesterday's woman — not young, her hair neatly done, the kind of person who remembers regular customers by name and new ones by their expression.
She recognized me right away.
"Morning. Didn't like the notebook?"
I took out the receipt and set it on the counter, not sure where to start.
"Can I ask you an odd question?"
She smiled — not out of politeness, but a real smile.
"Usually the oddest questions turn out to be the most interesting ones."
"This says I made thirty-one copies." I hesitated slightly. "But I don't remember doing that."
The woman took the receipt. Looked at it for a long time — unhurried, careful, the way you look at a document that doesn't add up but should.
"No," she said finally.
"Sorry?"
"You didn't make the copies."
She was completely certain. Without a shadow of doubt.
"Then why—"
"Another man made them."
I felt something clench inside me — sharply, as if someone had yanked the air out of the room.
"What other man?"
The woman closed her eyes for a second — I could see her honestly trying to reconstruct yesterday morning, pull it out of that part of memory where ordinary days get stacked up untidily.
"He came in literally a minute before you. I remember because the machine jammed the paper — I had to open the lid, and he was standing right there. Then you came in." She paused for a moment. "I thought you two knew each other."
"Why?"
"Because you said hello to him."
Helen glanced at me quickly. I felt her look — out of the corner of my eye, without turning my head.
"Did he answer?" she asked the shop assistant.
The woman shook her head apologetically.
"I don't know. I think… no."
"Do you remember his face?"
The woman was quiet for a long time. A very long time. Her look grew more and more lost — not frightened, just lost, the way you feel when you're reaching for a word and feel it slip away right out of your grasp.
"Strange…"
"What's strange?"
"I remembered it just a second ago…"
She closed her eyes. Rubbed her temples — carefully, with two fingers, like someone with a headache they've had so long they've stopped noticing it.
"I'm sorry. I can't. It's like… it smudged."
I looked at Helen. We both already knew this symptom. We didn't talk about it out loud — we just knew.
"What was he copying?" I asked.
The woman suddenly smiled — lightly, with the relief of someone finally asked a question they actually had an answer to.
"That, I do remember. Not documents. A notebook. A thick, black one. He copied almost the whole thing."
The blood drained from my face. I felt it physically — as if something warm had suddenly dropped away somewhere down inside me.
"Did he leave the original?"
"No. He took both the original and the copies."
We went outside.
The fog had thinned a little by then. London looked almost peaceful — an ordinary morning, ordinary people, a bus on the corner, a woman with a pram at the crossing. Nothing to suggest that right now, right here, something important was falling apart.
Helen was silent for a long time. Then she said quietly:
"If that wasn't you…"
"It was me."
She stopped.
"Just not today's me." I was surprised myself at how level my voice sounded. "Look at what we've got. My handwriting. My notes. Now the notebook. The man the shop assistant saw wasn't hiding. He was just living an ordinary day. Copying his notes. Buying stationery. Saying hello to people. Exactly the way I would."
Helen said nothing.
Because there was nothing left to argue with.
We were already about to leave when the shop assistant called out to us from the door.
"Excuse me!"
We turned around at the same moment. She was holding a small clear bag, holding it out across the threshold — a little awkwardly, like someone unsure they're doing the right thing but doing it anyway.
"I think this was left behind from him. I was cleaning around the machine, found it under the tray."
Inside the bag was a single sheet. Not a document, not a photograph. Just an ordinary test print — the kind made to check the copier's settings, then thrown away without a glance.
Almost the entire sheet was blank.
Only in the very bottom corner, where the edge of the original lands during a test feed, was there a cropped fragment of text. Three words, and nothing else — the rest of the sentence had been left forever outside the edge of the page.
…don't trust memory.
I stared at those three words for a long time.
Helen stood beside me, silent. Somewhere around the corner a car horn sounded. An elderly couple walked past — he was carrying two supermarket bags, she was saying something quietly, he nodded without answering.
The most frightening thing about that note wasn't the warning.
The most frightening thing was that I didn't know who it was addressed to. Had the past Michael left it for me — or for himself? Was it a reminder — or a confession?
I carefully folded the sheet and put it in my pocket.
Next to the receipt.
