title: Chapter 24
body:
The average person imagines human memory as a warehouse. A vast, dusty room full of shelves and numbered boxes. If some memory has gone missing, it means an outsider simply walked in, pulled the right box off a shelf, and carried it away. Pure mechanics, a break-in from outside.
For all these past weeks, I'd been living with exactly that convenient illusion. But now, looking at the blank pages, I was starting to understand: memory is fundamentally built differently.
It's more like an unbroken conversation with yourself. An inner monologue that runs for years and shapes what we call a personality. And once you stop trusting the person who was speaking inside your head yesterday, you automatically stop trusting your own thoughts today. The investigator and the suspect are locked inside the same body. The interrogation never ends.
I opened the black notebook again.
The first thirty pages were absolutely blank, not a single mark. The thirty-first opened with my own inked number in the top right corner. Thirty-two. Thirty-three. As if the first half of the book had been carefully removed from context by someone, without leaving a trace, without a seam.
I counted the sheets with my fingers — slowly, one by one. There was no mistake. Exactly thirty blanks.
Helen sat across from me. The pale light of her laptop lit up her profile — tired, focused. For the second hour now she'd been trying to run the watermarks and paper density of the anonymous notes against sealed databases. No leads. A complete dead end.
At some point she closed the laptop lid — a dry click in the silence — and looked at me over her glasses.
"Michael."
"Yes?"
"You noticed the strange part, didn't you?"
"Which one, out of all of them," I said with a wry smile, not looking up from the notebook.
She reached out, turned the notebook toward herself, and tapped a nail quietly against the blank field:
"Why exactly thirty-one pages? If someone — even the past you — wanted to destroy the start of the entries, why not just tear the pages out? Like with April in the old planner. Why leave them untouched?"
The question was so simple I didn't grasp its weight right away. In the world of archival cleanups — and Helen knew that world professionally, from the inside — there's one rule: if the goal is to destroy information, the medium disappears physically. Pages get torn out, burned, cut off at the root. They don't stay lying there untouched.
Here they were still in place. Perfectly clean. Neatly bound. As if someone, with a twisted kind of precision, wanted me to see exactly this — the vacuum itself, absence as a message.
I ran my palm over the paper. Thick, slightly rough, no traces of glue, no micro-cuts near the spine. A completely new object.
And then I tilted the notebook toward the window.
And stopped.
On the white, seemingly sterile surface, faint grooves emerged in the raking light. Relief shadows. Not ink — impression marks. When you write with a pen on a top sheet, the one underneath always remembers the movement of the nib. The paper had never seen pigment. But it remembered the motion.
"Helen."
She was on her feet instantly — from the tone of my voice, not the word.
"What is it?"
I turned the spread toward the light. We both held our breath.
Ten minutes later the kitchen table had turned into a makeshift forensics bench. No equipment. Just physics and a soft graphite pencil, found in a drawer among old batteries and manuals for appliances thrown out long ago.
I placed my palm on page thirty. My fingers trembled slightly — not from cold.
Very carefully, using the flat edge of the lead, I started shading the page in wide, even strokes. Graphite dust settled like grey haze, sinking into the cellulose fibers. Nothing at first. Just a flat, monotonous grey smear.
And then, in the grooves the pencil couldn't reach, the first white lines began to appear. Outlines. Broken arcs. The ghost of foreign text rising up from the bottom of the paper fiber.
I kept shading. Faster, denser.
Against the grey background, one word emerged distinctly, in relief — or rather, its cut-off ending.
"…ust"
The pencil slipped from my fingers. Rolled across the table with a dry clatter.
Helen leaned in so close I felt her breath. She said, quietly, almost soundlessly:
"'Trust'?"
I shook my head.
"Look at the length of the mark before the letters. The gap's too short for 'Tr—.'"
She straightened up slowly. Shifted her gaze to the clear bag lying at the edge of the table — the one we'd brought from the stationery shop a few hours earlier. The test print with its truncated line: "…don't trust memory."
Then back to the notebook. On the grey graphite field of page thirty, glowing in white relief: "…ust."
That man at the shop hadn't copied the line for the sake of a copy. He'd written it here. In this notebook. Pressing the pen down hard enough for the paper to bow, passing something through to the pages underneath — these thirty silent pages he'd deliberately left blank. Not to hide it. So that I'd find it exactly this way — through a layer, through resistance, through work.
Helen took off her glasses and rubbed the bridge of her nose for a long time. Then she asked quietly:
"How many times do you think he wrote it, on these thirty pages?"
I looked at the stack of untouched sheets.
"Thirty times," I said. "Once on each one."
She didn't answer. It didn't need one.
I closed my eyes. Breathed in the kitchen's damp air, deeply.
And for the first time in this whole investigation, I tried to reconstruct not a conspiracy, not Harris's secrets, not the architecture of the Protocol. I tried to picture myself, five years ago.
Not a frightened victim. Not a man being hunted. A man sitting at this table, completely calm, clear-headed, methodically writing the same line, page after page. He wasn't panicking. He wasn't rushing. He was simply doing what needed to be done — the way he always did, whenever code called for patience rather than inspiration.
He did it because, already then, in that torn-out April, he knew a day would come when his own memory would become his most dangerous enemy. Not the Protocol. Not the system. Himself.
The past Michael Lawson hadn't been leaving me breadcrumbs. He wasn't playing riddles. He was writing a survival manual — for a man who would have nothing left except what he could discover with his own hands.
And its first commandment had been burned into page thirty.
The first streetlights came on outside the window. London slid into evening with its usual indifference — noticing neither me, nor Helen, nor the thirty pages that had just stopped being blank.

title: Chapter 25
body:
The silence woke me.
Not the familiar city silence, the kind that is actually woven from hundreds of distant sirens, the hum of air conditioners, and heavy buses outside the window. A different one. Dense. Internal. As if during the night someone invisible had flipped a switch and shut off the constant, grinding noise of thoughts that had followed me through all these past weeks.
I lay still, eyes closed, listening to this new emptiness. Trying to guess what had changed while I slept.
Then I remembered. Thirty pages. Graphite dust. Three words rising up from the bottom of the paper fiber.
I sat up in bed.
The black notebook lay on the desk in the corner — in exactly the position I had left it in late that night. Beside it, a photograph turned face down. The plastic body of the camera. A cheap ballpoint pen. The physical world remained stable. And yet the underlying feeling was that someone had been in this flat again overnight and moved invisible markers around.
I walked over to the desk. The parquet was cold under my feet. I opened the notebook.
The first pages were my nervous, hurried notes, written in a state of half-panic:
"I remember school"
"I remember the first office in the City"
"I remember Amsterdam"
"I don't remember Thomas Harris"
"I don't remember October five years ago"
I turned the pages slowly. Page twenty. Twenty-one. Twenty-two. The handwriting changed by degrees — grew colder, the lines settled more evenly, letter by letter, without ragged tails. As if the person forming these words had, at some point, simply stopped panicking and pulled himself together.
I reached page thirty-one. Read it again. Then once more.
It wasn't about the handwriting. The handwriting was still mine. The language had changed.
On the first pages almost every entry began with shaky phrasing: "It seems to me…," "I think…," "It was probably like this…" That early-morning Michael doubted himself painfully, feeling for something solid, testing every step the way you test ice before you put your weight on it.
But further on, past the line of page thirty, the syntax snapped.
"Check the ministry archive"
"Don't call the old numbers"
"Save the source files"
"Destroy the physical copy"
"Wait"
No introductory words. No "I think" or "it seems to me." The author's personality had been washed out of the sentences — only the verbs remained. Short, clipped, ice-cold. These weren't reflections. They were orders.
I closed my eyes and leaned my forehead against the cool wall.
It had never occurred to me before that memory isn't only a warehouse of images, dates, and faces. Memory is also a way of thinking. A mental framework. An algorithm for processing incoming data. And that past Michael Lawson had been running that algorithm with a surgical precision that frightened me.
The doorbell rang. Two short bursts.
I didn't even go to check the peephole. I just knew.
Helen came in with two heavy supermarket bags, smelling of London damp and exhaust fumes. She dropped her jacket onto the hook — a practiced motion, no extra words — and walked through to the kitchen.
"Have you eaten?"
I shook my head.
"That's what I thought."
She started laying groceries out on the table: bread, butter, milk, pasta, a few green apples, a tin of ground coffee. I stood in the doorway and watched her precise, calm movements. She didn't ask where I kept the plates. Didn't hunt for the bread knife. She just reached out and opened the right cupboard.
"What?" she asked without turning around.
"Nothing."
"You're lying, Lawson. It's all over your face."
"It's just…" I faltered. "It looks as if you've always lived here. As if this is your space, not mine."
Helen stopped. For one second her fingers froze on the plastic lid of the butter dish. Then, just as calmly, without looking at me, she answered:
"Maybe a person gets used to taking care of someone else very quickly, Michael. When there's no one else left around."
And she went on unpacking the bag. That simple, pointedly domestic sentence hit my nerves harder than all our conversations about erased registries and abandoned bunkers.
The phone on the table vibrated briefly. Not mine — hers.
Helen glanced down at the screen. A notification had lit up on the locked display — two Latin letters and a single line of text.
Mo: "Hope you're okay."
She turned the phone face down. Too fast.
But I had already read it. My eyes had caught the line in a fraction of a second — a professional habit you can't shake.
She understood that from my face. For a few seconds we stood in complete silence.
"A friend?" I asked carefully.
She gave a vague nod, looking at her hands.
"Yes. Something like that."
"From Dubai?"
"Yes." Quietly. "From Dubai."
"Have you known each other long?"
"Almost a year."
I didn't ask anything more. She didn't explain either. Only when Helen went over to the stove to put the kettle on did she say, very quietly — almost into the air, almost to herself:
"Sometimes you badly want to trust a person you've never met face to face. Simply because there's no one left to trust in your own world."
I looked at her tense back.
"And how's that going? Does it work?"
She let out a short, dry laugh.
"So far all I manage is to keep myself in check and answer him a few hours late."
That was as far as the conversation went. We drank coffee, and for some reason it felt to me that none of it had really been about Dubai, or about a man named Mo. Helen was running her own game against the Protocol — parallel, autonomous. And the stakes in it were no lower than mine.
Closer to two she left — to check paper specifications at the audit center.
The flat sank back into silence.
I went back to the desk, opened the notebook, and started reading it differently. Not as a diary. As an interrogation transcript. My own interrogation.
I took a blank sheet and methodically copied out every directive verb that appeared after page thirty. It came out as a strange list:
"Check"
"Seal the perimeter"
"Don't open files without encryption"
"Wait for the signal"
"DON'T DEVELOP"
"Don't explain"
My hand stopped at the last phrase.
"Don't explain." I didn't remember writing it. Didn't remember the circumstances. And above all — I didn't understand who exactly the order was addressed to. Myself? Harris, in that torn-out April? Or the future Michael Lawson, who would one day crack the cover of an old planner and start frantically poring over graphite traces?
The shadows of the window frames crept across the floor, stretching into long dark bands. Evening was coming on outside — indifferent, as always, without warning.
And it was right then, in the thickening dusk, that I clearly grasped one thing.
All those last, clipped pages had been written by a man who already knew the ending. He had calculated every step, seen the whole picture, top to bottom. And I was still wandering in the dark.
I slowly closed the notebook and laid my palm on the cold black cover.
For the first time in the whole investigation, what I felt was fear — not of the Protocol, not of the intelligence services, not of someone from outside stealing what was left of my digital life.
I had begun to fear the man who once owned that life. My past self. Because with every page I read, I came to know him better. And understood less and less whether I ever wanted to become him again.

title: Chapter 26
body:
That day, for the first time, we weren't driving after a ghost.
Not after a witness, not after a hiding place, not after another notebook with its pages torn out. We were driving to look for me. The version of me that paid bills, withdrew cash, and left traces in banking logs — while I calmly remembered none of it.
"Where are we going?" Helen asked as I started the engine.
The old diesel estate car rumbled dully to life, shuddering through its whole body. Beyond the windscreen the wipers smeared away the last of the morning drizzle.
"To the bank."
She turned to me:
"What for?"
"Memory lies. Registries get rewritten. Databases get reformatted." I put it in gear. "But money almost never lies. The system guards its transactions better than it guards human lives."
"You already tried that. In the first few days."
I said nothing. She was right — I had tried. "Our database shows that you have never been a client of this bank." I remembered that sentence word for word.
"That was the front end," Helen said, looking straight ahead. "The online registry, the first layer. That's where the Protocol reaches first — it's fast and clean. But at the big banks the transaction archives are kept separately. Physically. On backup servers with a sync lag of up to several weeks. Accounting doesn't like it when someone digs around in its territory without authorization."
"You think the archive is untouched?"
"I think they don't have a single master switch." She took a small slip of paper out of her coat pocket — some printed branch code with an address. "And I think we don't need the central office. We need a branch that still runs on the old processing system. I found one."
Helen added nothing more. She silently pulled the seatbelt across and clicked the buckle home.
London was going about its usual, deafeningly ordinary life. Red buses crawled heavily through the jam on Oxford Street. Bike couriers shot across junctions on a flashing red. On the corners, clerks in identical suits drank coffee — one arguing on the phone, another laughing. An ordinary Wednesday morning that couldn't have cared less about us.
At moments like that I started to feel as if our whole story with the Protocol existed solely inside two skulls — mine and Helen's. As if the huge city were simply turning its gears, not noticing that somewhere on its edges the fabric of someone's reality was slowly coming apart.
We parked in a narrow side street beside the bank's brick building. I had been its client for more than ten years — going back to the days of the first office in the City.
Automatic glass doors. A metal-detector frame. A short, lazy queue at the terminals. It was probably the most boring place in London. Which was exactly why it felt safe to me.
The woman behind the counter — corporate badge, the name "Sarah" — glanced quickly at my passport and smiled at once.
"Good morning, Mr Lawson. How can I help?"
A living person. Not an empty line in a national-insurance database. I caught myself noticing that this now mattered.
"I need a paper statement covering all accounts and transactions for the last five years. With the fullest possible detail on points of sale and branches."
She raised her eyebrows:
"Five years? We'll have to pull the deep archive logs. That'll take a while."
"I'll wait."
While Sarah keyed in the query parameters, I let my eyes drift around the hall. An elderly man in horn-rimmed glasses was filling out a transfer slip. A young couple with a pram were quietly arguing by the cash machine. The guard at the entrance was drinking coffee from a paper cup, watching the street through the glass. For the first time in days the tight coil of anxiety in my chest eased a little.
About ten minutes later Sarah came back with a hefty stack of paper held together by a plastic clip.
"It's absolutely everything, sir. Every debit, every penny."
Helen and I settled at a round table at the back of the hall — well away from other eyes.
I started leafing through slowly, page by page, moving backwards through time. Salary payments from old clients. Utility debits. Supermarket purchases. Petrol stations. Pub tabs. An ordinary, utterly unremarkable life of a single IT man.
October. Five years ago.
I stopped.
The fourteenth. The fifteenth. The sixteenth.
Three days in a row — not a single transaction. None at all. No cash withdrawn from a machine. No morning sandwich bought. No Tube fare paid. The card had gone dead for those seventy-two hours. Three sterile days that had dropped out of the financial record.
"Strange," Helen said quietly, peering into the empty gaps between the dates.
"I never once stayed home three days straight without going out."
On the fourth day, the seventeenth of October, the first and only entry appeared.
Cash withdrawal. £3,000. Branch teller.
Helen looked at me sharply:
"Have you ever withdrawn sums like that in cash?"
"Never." I set the page down. "I have a pathological aversion to cash. All my contracts, all my personal spending — always digital. Three thousand pounds in notes is absurd. I simply had no reason to take it out."
I stood up and walked over to the counter.
"Sarah. One more question. Can you pull the camera footage from that day? Or at least find out which branch, exactly, the transaction went through?"
She shook her head gently:
"The video won't be possible, sir. Security footage is kept for ninety days, then automatically overwritten. Standard confidentiality protocol."
"And the branch address?"
"That I can check right now."
Her fingers ran across the keyboard. The log opened. Sarah studied the line — and something in her face changed. Just slightly. Her brows drew together a little. Her finger froze on the mouse.
"Everything all right?" I asked.
She read the line again. Frowned.
"Yes… I mean, no. It's a bit odd."
"What exactly?"
She turned the monitor a little toward me:
"According to the transaction's system history, those three thousand pounds were paid out to you five years ago... here. In this very branch, at this counter."
I looked slowly around. High ceilings. New air conditioners. White plastic counters.
"That's physically impossible, Sarah."
"Why? The branch code matches to the last digit."
"Because five years ago this building didn't exist here. It was built two years ago, after the whole square was redeveloped. I know that for certain."
She looked back and forth between me and the screen for a few seconds. Then she said quietly:
"Mr Lawson... according to our corporate property registry, our branch has operated continuously at this address for eleven years. Since the shopping quarter was founded."
We stepped out onto the street in complete silence.
I stopped on the pavement and turned back. Huge glass shopfronts. A metal logo above the entrance. Flawless automatic doors letting people in and out. All of it looked monolithic and natural — as if it had stood here since London itself was built.
"Michael... are you sure?" Helen asked quietly, wrapping herself in her scarf. "Absolutely sure?"
"Absolutely."
"Maybe you're mixing up the junctions? Five years is a long time, the topography of the City changes..."
"No."
I closed my eyes.
And behind my eyelids, with cinematic clarity, a completely different picture rose up. A small secondhand bookshop that had stood on exactly this spot. Dark wooden shelves to the ceiling. The heavy, cosy smell of old paper and leather bindings. A grey-haired, slightly deaf old man in a corduroy jacket who always set aside, under the counter, the newest titles on cryptography and distributed-systems architecture.
I remembered that shop down to the smallest details. The creak of the third floorboard by the entrance. The chip on the handle of the front door. The taste of the mint sweets the old man offered his rare customers.
I opened my eyes. Where the wooden shelves had been, there stood cold self-service terminals.
"Michael," Helen's voice wavered. "Are you sure..." she faltered.
"Finish it."
"Are you sure that memory of the bookshop... belongs to you at all?"
I didn't answer.
Not because I didn't want to. Because for the first time in the whole investigation the words physically wouldn't come. Until today I had doubted documents. Then I had started doubting my own memory. But now, looking at the shining façade of the bank, I ran up against a thought my brain had never let through before — it had thrown up protective blocks, kept me away from it.
What if some of my memories — vivid, tangible, detailed, with a smell and a taste — had never belonged to me? What if the Protocol doesn't just erase lives, but transplants fragments of other people's memory into those left behind in the void?
Helen stood beside me and said nothing.
On the corner, by the newspaper kiosk, a passer-by coughed — short, rasping, into the collar of his coat. I raised my head.
The street was empty.

title: Chapter 27
body:
We spent the drive back in silence.
The old diesel engine droned monotonously under the bonnet, but the sound no longer soothed me. After the visit to the bank, the huge city of London had started to feel like a stage set to me. Not because the buildings had changed shape or the streets had gone crooked — no, the double-deckers were still hopelessly off schedule, the bike couriers still swore savagely at cab drivers. Something else had changed. My internal coordinate system.
Before, whenever I fell into another gap of forgetting, I could at least allow for the existence of some firm point to stand on. A document. A mark in a registry. A tangible memory. Now the Protocol had knocked that last foundation out from under me too. If memory can be contraband — if it can belong to someone else — then what in this life is even mine? Is this my jacket? Is this my name?
Helen asked to be dropped at her building — a small, darkened brick five-storey block in one of those quiet, half-asleep neighbourhoods tucked between Victoria and Pimlico.
"Coming up?" she asked unexpectedly, once I'd killed the engine.
Her pale face didn't have its usual mask of archival severity. Only tiredness — a dull, human tiredness.
I was surprised. In all the weeks of the investigation she had never once let me into her personal space. We met on neutral ground: cheap cafés, railway stations, damp archive basements.
"If I won't be in the way."
She smiled faintly, opening the door:
"Michael, in our situation it's already pretty hard to be in anyone's way. There's barely anything left of us as it is."
Helen's flat turned out to be exactly as I'd pictured it — spare, functional, free of domestic clutter. A small living room combined with a dining area. Dense rows of bookshelves crammed with heavy reference volumes. A few cardboard boxes with archive labels against the wall. A massive wooden table under stacks of printouts.
And an enormous, almost anomalous number of houseplants.
I automatically counted the pots on the wide windowsill. Six identical clay containers. Two of them stood empty — dead stems, cut off at the root, poking out of the dry grey soil. The other four plants were tended with pedantic care, as if someone watched over them daily, checking against a timer.
Two dead. Four alive. I didn't ask when the first two had died.
"Coffee?" came from the tiny kitchen.
"Strong, if you can."
While she fussed with the moka pot, I walked slowly around the room. No personal things. No holiday souvenirs, no postcards on the fridge, no family portraits. As if the person deliberately avoided leaving lasting traces of her own presence in this world.
Only by the sofa, on a low coffee table, stood a small wooden frame. Face down.
My eyes slid over it, but I didn't touch it. Every condemned person is entitled to their own locked safe.
"Here." Helen set a heavy ceramic mug in front of me.
I took a sip. Black, thick, scalding — with a bitter aftertaste of dark chocolate. Almost the same as the coffee the old photographer used to brew in Camden.
"Have you lived here long?" I asked, to break the silence closing in.
"Seven years."
"Do you like the area?"
She shrugged, looking somewhere through me:
"I don't know anymore. Honestly — I don't know."
It sounded too broken for a simple question about a neighbourhood.
The phone on the table spun a short arc on the polished wood. A vibration. The screen had ended up turned toward me, and I read the sender's name automatically.
Mo: "Did you eat today?"
Helen stared for a long time, without moving, at the glowing rectangle — as if it posed a physical threat. Then she picked up the phone, unlocked it. Quickly typed a few words. Stopped. Deleted them. Raised her fingers over the keyboard again, wrote something, frowned, and destroyed the text again. In the end she just locked the screen and set the phone down, having sent nothing at all.
"Sorry," she said quietly.
"Don't apologize. I understand completely."
She buried her fingers in her hair, sat silent for a minute. Then she suddenly lifted her head:
"Have you ever been to Dubai, Lawson?"
"No. Why?"
"Me neither. Never in my life."
A bitter pause.
"Funny, isn't it? A person you've never seen face to face, who doesn't exist in your tangible world — sometimes he knows more about the structure of your day than the people across the landing."
"Who is he, Helen?"
She turned the cooling mug in her fingers for a long time.
"Just a person. From the Network."
I allowed myself a faint smile:
"Speaking as a systems architect: after the phrase 'just a person,' the logs usually start showing the worst, most unsolvable software failure of all."
For the first time in days Helen laughed — short, genuine, as if frightened by her own reaction. And immediately went serious again.
"You may be right." She looked down into the dark bottom of the coffee. "He's a civil architect. Designs glass-and-concrete towers somewhere in the Emirates. We met on a half-forgotten forum almost a year ago. At first we argued about urban planning, about dead zones in architecture. Then we started talking about everything else. About life. About fears."
"And?"
"And nothing." She hesitated a little. "Sometimes I feel I know the structure of his soul better than the character of anyone I work with at the department. And then I come to my senses and remember that I've never in my life heard this man laugh for real. Not a written 'ha-ha' — an actual voice. I don't know how he walks. How he goes quiet when he's angry. The internet is a terrifying thing, Michael. It's far too brilliant at filling people in inside our heads, plugging the emptiness with perfect illusions."
I said nothing. I had nothing to argue with. For all these past weeks I had been doing exactly the same thing — trying to reconstruct the image of a man out of digital scraps, old logs, and other people's receipts. And every time, instead of a living Michael Lawson, I got a cold, flawless simulation.
When I had already stood up to leave, my eyes caught again, involuntarily, on the wooden frame by the sofa.
Helen registered the movement. Silently she went over to the table, slowly turned the frame over, and looked at the photo for a few seconds. Then she held it out to me.
In the photograph was a young, laughing woman of about twenty-five. A light summer dress. In her arms — a huge, ridiculous bouquet of sunflowers. Sunlight flooded the frame. To her right stood a man — jeans, a light jacket.
His face wasn't there. The right edge of the photo had been cut off. Brutally, but frighteningly straight — with a utility knife, almost along a ruler.
"Your sister?" I asked.
"No."
"A friend?"
Helen slowly shook her head:
"It's me, Michael. The photo was taken six years ago in Kent."
I moved my gaze from the photograph to her. The same line of the jaw. The same shape of the eyes. But in the eyes in the photo there was something the present Helen no longer had — a lightness you can't act.
"And the man beside you?"
She was silent for so long that outside the window a scheduled bus had time to pull in and drive away.
"I don't know," she answered at last. Calmly. Without a shadow of performance.
"What do you mean, you don't know? It's your own photograph, Helen."
"In the most literal sense. I remember sitting at this table with a utility knife and cutting off the right part of the frame with my own hands. I did it deliberately. But I absolutely do not remember who was standing there. What colour his hair was. What his name was. It's all gone."
We stood facing each other in the half-dark of the flat, and a thought struck me that was absurd in its simplicity.
Until today I had selfishly assumed this whole nightmare was happening only to me. That it was my life the Protocol was methodically tearing pages out of. But now I could see that someone had already cut an enormous piece out of the living flesh of Helen's life with the very same sterile shears. By the same algorithm. With identical neatness.
22:15
Late that evening, back in the empty flat, I walked on autopilot to the desk and put on the headset.
Over the past weeks this little plastic device had become as obligatory an attribute as a wristwatch or a set of keys. I no longer thought about why I put it on. I just put it on — and it eased a little.
I dropped my head back onto the leather headrest of the chair. For a few seconds a dense, dead silence filled the earpiece. Then, somewhere near my right temple, a relay clicked, barely audible.
"Michael?" Clara's voice came through full and soft, without a single electronic flatness. "This is the longest you've stayed silent in one day. The logs record no queries for almost three hours."
"Is that a critical error?"
A tiny pause — barely noticeable, as if she were gathering her thoughts.
"I don't know. But usually you fall into that kind of silence exactly when you're getting close to some right question."
I closed my eyes. The arm of the headset pressed lightly on the bone behind my ear.
"Clara... What if I'm no longer sure it's really me asking all these questions? What if someone else is speaking inside me?"
Silence.
A long one. Far longer than the standard wait time. So drawn out that I'd already decided the signal had dropped, that the micro-battery in the arm had died.
Then Clara said — very quietly, stripping her voice of its usual lightness:
"In that case, Michael... maybe it's finally time to stop looking for the one who remembers all this. And to try to find the one who, at some point, consciously decided to forget it."
There was a dry crack in my ear. The connection cut out.
I slowly took off the headset and set it on the desk. I sat in the dark until my eyes adjusted.
And only then did I understand what was bothering me.
For the first time in all our daily conversations, Clara hadn't made a joke at the end. Hadn't smoothed the edges with a routine barb. Hadn't said her usual: "Talk soon, Lawson."
As if my question hadn't been provided for in her software architecture.
Or as if the answer to it lay far beyond what she was permitted to tell me.

title: Chapter 28
body:
By evening the rain had finally worn itself out.
After several days of unbroken damp, London was slowly getting its outlines back. In the puddles on the asphalt, upside-down reflections of red buses trembled. Neon signs flickered on above café doorways. For the first time the air stopped smelling only of wet stone and petrol — some space had opened up in it.
I walked home on foot through Pimlico. Not because I wanted a stroll. I just desperately needed time — to fit into my head what had happened at the bank and in Helen's flat.
For the past day I'd kept catching myself on one obsessive thought: the investigation had finally stopped moving forward, stopped widening its geography. Instead it had changed vector and was now boring inward at a frightening speed. Every till receipt, every pressed groove in paper told me nothing about a conspiracy of corporations or about the Protocol. They told me about myself. About the man who had lived in my body before I switched on inside it.
Climbing the dark stairwell that smelled of old wood, I took the headset out of my pocket with a movement worn down to pure automatism and put it on my right ear. The arm gripped the bone tightly behind the shell of the ear.
For a few seconds a velvet silence filled the earpiece. Then, near my temple, a relay clicked delicately.
"Good evening, Michael."
Clara's voice — full, soft, with a faint sly note in it. The way someone sounds when they're glad to hear you.
"Hi, Clara."
"Judging by the background noise and the lack of low-frequency vibration... you're without the car today?"
"Good guess."
"Not a guess at all." She gave a quiet chuckle. "I can just hear the echo of the stairwell in your building. And you're breathing hard."
I smiled despite myself, turning the key in the lock.
And caught myself doing it at once — smiling at an invisible voice in my ear. Over these past years I'd got used to smiling at it as naturally and openly as I once, in my past life, smiled at living people. It no longer seemed strange to me. That, probably, was exactly what should have set off an alarm.
"What have you been doing all day?" she asked while I took my shoes off in the hall.
"Learning all over again to be afraid of my own handwriting, and to doubt whether the third floorboard of a secondhand bookshop was ever real."
"Sounds intriguing and extremely productive."
"I don't think so. Actually — not really."
"Then tell me. I'm listening."
I filled the kettle, clicked the switch. While the appliance began its quiet whine, warming the element, I recounted it all briefly, without extra emotion. The bank statement. The three empty days in October. The nonexistent branch that, on paper, had stood on the site of the bookshop for eleven years. The new notebook with its pressed-in "…rust." The cut-off photo in Helen's flat. The messages from the contact "Mo."
Clara listened with astonishing attention. She barely interrupted. She dropped none of her usual sarcastic remarks — only now and then asked short, pinpoint questions. Very precise technically and deep at the same time. Exactly the kind of questions asked by people who aren't just studying your problem from outside but have known you yourself — your triggers, your habits, your blind spots — for a very long time.
When I finished, a cotton-wool silence hung in the flat. The only sound was the water coming to a boil on the stove.
"You know, Michael..." Clara broke the silence.
"What?"
"You've changed a great deal."
"You mean I've degraded?"
"No." A short pause — as if she were choosing a metaphor. "Over the course of today."
I smirked, lifting the kettle off:
"And which way did I get bent?"
"Before, when you'd only just found the hidden layer in the old planner, you were furiously hunting for someone to blame. You behaved like a classic victim of persecution. And now... now you're looking for the truth. Even knowing you might not like it. Those are fundamentally different operating modes, Michael."
I poured a mug, went to the window, and leaned my shoulder against the frame. Beyond the glass London was slowly sinking into evening. Blurred lights. The silhouettes of trees in Pimlico. Somewhere below, a bus hummed steadily.
We stayed silent for a few minutes. Just like that — sharing the quiet between the two of us over an encrypted radio channel, and I felt no awkwardness about it. That, probably, was what should have set off an alarm too.
And suddenly, obeying some deep impulse, I said quietly into the microphone:
"Thank you."
In the earpiece — a second's hesitation. Barely noticeable.
"For what, Michael? I'm only doing my..."
"For still talking to me," I cut her off. "No joking, Clara. If I'm being completely honest... I have no idea who I'd be in the middle of this disintegrating world without your voice in this damn headset. I'm in your debt."
And then came silence.
Not the kind that happens when someone is moved and searching for words. Not the kind that comes from awkwardness or fatigue. This was a different silence — sterile, deafening. As if at the other end of the line not only the voice had vanished in a single second, but the very background noise of the channel. The interference. The mic hum. Everything alive.
One second. Two. Three.
I slowly raised my hand, took off the headset, and stared at the matte body of it in my palm — dully, the way you stare at a thing that has just stopped being what it seemed to be.
And right there in my palm, from the tiny bone-conduction speaker, came a dry electronic click.
And then — a voice. Not her voice. A different one. Stripped of intonation, of overtones, of breath. Stripped of everything that makes a sound human.
"Request processed."
A pause an eternity long.
"Expression of thanks logged in the session system journal."
I didn't move. My fingers were going wooden. My heart was pounding somewhere around my throat.
I slowly put the headset back in place.
"Clara?" my voice cracked to a rasp.
Silence.
"Clara. This isn't funny. Answer me."
Silence.
I was already about to rip the device off and hurl it at the wall — and at that exact moment the familiar voice came back on the air. Soft. Warm. With a living depth to it. As if nothing had happened.
"Sorry, Michael. The connection dropped for a second, the base relay threw a packet error. London's towers, reliable as ever."
I frowned hard.
"Is everything really all right on your end?"
She answered almost at once. But there was something wrong in that instant speed. Too smooth. Too even.
"Of course. Everything's operating normally. Why do you ask?"
"Did you hear what happened on the line? Just now."
A microscopic delay — less than a second:
"What exactly?"
"Instead of you, the earpiece was speaking with..." I broke off.
I stared into the darkness beyond the window. Because it had suddenly become physically hard to find the words. What exactly had I heard? A male voice? A female one? A synthesis? I was no longer sure. My brain, defending itself, was trying to blur that memory — swap it for ordinary radio noise, a technical glitch, tiredness.
"Nothing, Clara. Forget it. Must have imagined it. Nerves."
"Must have," she agreed.
Without irony. Too calm. Too fast.
And for the first time in all our acquaintance it seemed to me that in this game I wasn't the only one hiding something from the outside world.
23:40
Late that night I opened the laptop. Mechanically, with no clear aim — I just needed to keep my hands busy.
On the screen, among the inactive windows, an old service page was still open: the headset's wireless-connection history. Normally I never looked in there — the device worked fine, there was no need. But tonight something — some animal instinct — made me scroll the log all the way to the bottom.
The line of the last connection. Time: 19:42.
In the connection-status field it read:
"Session resumed."
And right below it, in the small grey type of a system debugger:
"Operator unavailable. Subsystem simulated via core profile."
I read the line five times. Then once more. Until the letters began to swim before my eyes.
The operator had been unavailable. The subsystem had been simulated through the core profile.
I hit F5. The script reloaded. The grey text disappeared — replaced by the standard green marker of a stable connection. As if it had never existed. As if the system had shown me its guts for a fraction of a second and then tidied up the traces after itself.
I slowly closed the laptop lid.
I sat in the dark.
And didn't let myself think what I was already thinking. Didn't let the thought take shape in words, because I knew: the moment it took shape, there would be no way back.
But it came anyway. Quietly, inescapably, the way the most terrible things always do.
What if, all these weeks, months, years — the one talking to me at the other end of the line hadn't been the living, breathing, ironic person I was used to calling Clara at all?
What if a plain human "thank you" had simply overloaded the buffer — and for three seconds a soulless machine had shown its real face?
Outside the window London made its noise. A passer-by coughed below — rasping, short, into the collar of his coat.
I didn't raise my head.

title: Chapter 29
body:
The next morning I was woken by the phone.
Not a sharp ring — just a short, dry click of an incoming notification. I hadn't yet fully surfaced from a heavy, dreamless sleep when I reached for the bedside table and saw the sender's name on the display.
Helen.
The message was a single sentence, with no punctuation at the end:
"I need a witness today"
I read it three times, trying, through the last of my drowsiness, to catch the exact syntactic weight of the words. Not "I need help." Not "come quickly." That precise wording — legally measured and detached. A witness.
I typed back:
"What happened?"
Her reply dropped instantly, as if she'd been holding her finger over the keyboard, waiting for my reaction:
"Just come."
Forty minutes later I was parking outside her building in Pimlico.
Helen opened the door almost at once, the moment I touched the bell. She looked as though she hadn't just gone without sleep that night but hadn't slept for the past week — pale, with sharp shadows at the corners of her mouth. But it wasn't the tiredness that frightened me. A new, alarmingly composed hardness had come into her movements. She held herself like someone who had hesitated a long time at the edge of a cliff — and finally reached a final decision.
"Come in," she said shortly, stepping back into the hall.
The flat looked almost the same as the day before. Almost. My systems eye instantly registered the changes in the geometry of the room. On the massive wooden table stood three neat stacks of documents. On the floor stood a black plastic rubbish bag. On a chair — a small office shredder with an empty bin, glinting dully in the morning light.
I stopped in the middle of the living room.
"Will you explain what's going on?"
"Yes. Right now."
She went over to the first stack and picked up the top sheet in its stiff cardboard cover.
"My university documents. My degree from the London School of Economics. Archive extracts. Professors' references. A certificate of my placement at the ministry."
She opened the folder — inside lay immaculately preserved sheets, slightly yellowed with age, watermarked.
"Last night, after you left, I did an audit. I decided to check how many physical, tangible documents of my existence were still left in this reality."
A short pause.
"It turned out to be considerably fewer than I'd assumed."
She held out the degree certificate to me. I took it — examined it. Her name. State seals. The panel's signatures. The typeface, the embossing — it all looked weighty and genuine.
"I don't see anything wrong."
"Turn the sheet over."
I turned it. An utterly blank white surface looked back at me.
"In my graduation year the university registry put a purple ink stamp on the back of the form — a through-registration into the national education registry," she rapped out. "Without it this document is just pretty print work. The stamp is gone. Not rubbed off. Not bleached out. It's simply... not there anymore."
"Maybe a different form of the certificate for your cohort?"
"No. At three in the morning I wrote to a coursemate in Edinburgh. She sent a copy of her own degree. The stamp is there."
Helen opened the second folder.
"The tenancy agreement for this flat. The current contract."
I ran my eyes over the standard clauses. Signatures. The deposit amount. The exact address. Everything looked flawless, until my fingers turned the page with the particulars.
In the field "Emergency contact person" there was a blank inked dash.
"There was no one at all at the time of signing?" I asked, looking at that forlorn emptiness.
Helen stared for a long time out the window, where drops of morning rain crept slowly down the glass.
"There was," she said quietly at last.
"Who?"
She closed her eyes. Her lashes trembled.
"I don't remember, Michael."
Those three words were spoken with such everyday calm that it frightened me more than if she had burst into tears. It was a dry statement of a system failure — not a complaint, not a cry. Just a fact.
She went to the bookcase and took out a heavy photo album in worn velvet. She set it on the table in front of me and opened it to the middle.
I started leafing through. A childhood in the south of England. School trips. Student journeys around Europe. Ministry interiors with colleagues. A perfectly ordinary, warm human life — until my eye snagged on one recurring oddity.
In every group or paired photo, too much free, compositionally unjustified space was left beside Helen. The frame seemed to tilt to one side. As if the photographer had originally centred the composition for two — but the second person, for some reason, hadn't come into focus. Or had evaporated.
I raised my eyes to her.
"Is this what I think it is?"
"Yes." She snapped the album shut with a dull thud. "But there's a difference. I checked the original negatives. These photographs were never cropped. They came off the printer like this from the very first day."
I looked again at the closed cover.
In all those shots Helen stood a little left of centre. And in all of them she was looking not into the lens but slightly up and to the right — at someone standing next to her. At someone the system had already managed to cut completely out of the very structure of space.
"That's why I wrote to you this morning." Helen drew a deep breath, her shoulders dropping a little. "I need a witness, Michael."
"A witness for what?"
She moved away to the window. Leaned her forehead against the cool glass, staring for a long time into the grey, deserted street.
"If one day I start insisting that I've lived in this flat completely alone my whole life... that I never had any friends, anyone close, any memory of another person's footsteps in this room..."
She turned sharply, and her eyes flashed.
"Don't believe me. Do you hear? Don't believe today's me."
"Helen, stop it. We'll find a way out. The Protocol can be..."
"Promise me, Michael."
"Don't talk as if they're already erasing you."
"Promise."
She raised her voice — only a little, by a semitone. But that fleeting show of living, desperate human will was enough to catch the breath in my throat.
I slowly nodded.
"I promise. I'll remember."
She exhaled — raggedly, with relief, as if something heavy had been lifted off her chest. As if this pledge, this fixing of the fact by an outside observer, was exactly what she'd been waiting for all night.
We sat a long time in her quiet kitchen, looking silently into our cups. For about twenty minutes neither of us dared break the silence. Outside, the rain dripped. On the windowsill stood four living and two dead plants in identical clay pots. I tried not to look at the dead ones.
"Do you know what's the most frightening thing in all of this?" she finally asked quietly, without lifting her head.
"What?"
"I've caught myself thinking that I'm no longer afraid at all of disappearing physically. Or of losing my name."
I looked carefully at her pale profile.
"Then what are you afraid of?"
She smiled — very quietly, very sadly. The smile of someone who has already settled some important question and become, because of it, both calmer and further away.
"I'm afraid that one day my own disappearance will seem to me... something completely normal. The natural order of things."
At that moment the phone on the windowsill vibrated briefly. The screen flared, cutting through the half-dark of the kitchen.
Mo: "I dreamed about you tonight."
Helen's eyes slid over the glowing letters. And her face changed — instantly, the way the light changes when the sun comes out from behind clouds. She smiled so warmly and openly as I had never seen in all the days of our shared race. In that smile, for a second, the very twenty-five-year-old girl from the Kent photo showed through — with the bouquet of sunflowers, flooded with light.
Then she slowly reached out, turned the phone face down, and locked it.
Without answering a thing.
I tactfully kept quiet. But in that very second, looking at her lowered shoulders, I understood one simple thing with merciless clarity.
If the Protocol erases a person gradually, layer by layer — that distant, invisible architect from Dubai is right now exchanging messages with a woman who, perhaps in just a few weeks, will physically no longer remember why she ever decided to answer his first message.
And he'll go on writing. Because he won't know.
Late that evening, back in my own empty flat, I took a new black notebook out of the desk drawer.
I opened it to a blank page. I stared a long time at the white emptiness, cradling the pen in my fingers. Then I wrote a sentence — for the first time in all this time not about myself, not about my erased years, not about my own private fears:
"If I ever forget Helen, it will mean that I'm not the only one who has lost this war."
I put a full stop. Closed the notebook.
And only as I was putting the pen away did I notice the thing that sent a short spasm through my body.
I had written that sentence in exactly the same cold, even, almost calligraphic hand — the one that filled the directive pages after the thirtieth. That alien hand whose manner I was subconsciously adopting more with every day, and feared more and more.
I looked at my own letters for a long time.
Then — for the first time in the whole investigation — I didn't cross them out.

title: Chapter 30
body:
That evening, for the first time in all this time, I switched the phone off completely.
Not onto silent. Not just the internet off. I actually held down the side button, waited for the system slider, and shut the device down. The screen blinked and went dark — a slab of dead black glass.
An unnatural, dense silence settled over the flat at once. I'd never thought before about how many times a day I reach for my pocket on autopilot — to check my inbox, look through logs, make sure the world hasn't changed without my knowledge. As if somewhere in my subconscious sat an infantile certainty: if you keep staring at the glowing rectangle, reality won't dare rearrange itself.
Now I knew for a fact — it would. A second is all it needs, while you blink.
I went over to the bookcase in the corner of the living room.
The upper shelves held dense rows of technical books I'd collected over years. Distributed computing. Fault-tolerant network architecture. Applied cryptography. Once those spines had given me a professional pride — markers of competence, proof that I knew how complex systems were built. Now they produced only a dull embarrassment. It turned out I could administer other people's architectures but had completely failed to protect my own identity.
I ran my fingertips along the rough cardboard until one of the books felt subjectively heavier than the rest. An old university textbook on distributed systems. When I pulled it off the shelf, a narrow slip of paper, folded in half, slid quietly out of the centre of the block with a soft rustle.
An ordinary till receipt from an electronics supermarket.
I picked it up off the floor. The date — June, six years ago. A year before that damned October. Before Harris. Before the Protocol. In the lower part of the receipt were three line items:
Study manual — 1 pc.
Fineliner pen (black) — 1 pc.
Kodak Professional 400 film (35 mm) — 1 pc.
I stared at that dot-matrix line for a long time.
So, long before any of it — before the anonymous notes, before the nighttime escapes, before the archive bunkers — I had already been buying professional photographic film. Why? I'd never had any interest in analogue photography. The camera in my phone had always fully covered my needs. A casual snapshot for memory's sake, nothing more.
I turned the receipt over. The back was blank. But the thermal paper itself looked deformed — as if it had been folded and unfolded many times, with maniacal precision, along the same axes.
I flattened the sheet and held it up to the desk lamp. At a certain angle a faint dent showed through in the middle of the paper field. The pigment had long since evaporated, but the relief trace of a hard pen stroke remained.
I took a graphite pencil out of the drawer and began carefully, barely touching the surface, to shade the paper with horizontal strokes. White outlines started to emerge from under the grey haze — first one broken line, then a vertical stroke, then a whole short phrase. In my own sweeping, angular hand:
"If you start to have doubts — stop."
Seven words. No date, no explanation, no signature. Just a dry mental veto, suspended in a vacuum.
There was a quiet knock at the door. Three calm, measured raps with the knuckles — not the electric bell, but exactly that, in the human way.
I flinched, set the receipt aside, and went to open it.
On the landing, under the dim corridor light, stood Helen. She was clutching a kraft paper bag to her chest.
"Sorry," she said quietly, walking past me. "I didn't warn you. Your phone's off."
"Has something happened?"
She shook her head and gave a faint smile, nodding at the bag:
"Just dinner. From the nearest Chinatown."
"This is starting to become a habit with you."
"One of the two of us ought to have at least some stable domestic habit," she replied, already from the kitchen.
We ate in silence, straight out of the cardboard cartons, to the monotonous noise of the kettle coming to a boil. For about ten minutes neither of us broke the quiet. Outside, London was slowly going into night — no hurry, no announcements, just one streetlamp going out after another.
Then Helen set down her chopsticks and looked at me. Her gaze was unusually focused — the way people look when they've finally resolved to say something they've held in for a long time.
"Today I caught myself in a feeling, Michael. Not even a thought — a physical feeling."
"What feeling?"
She turned the clear plastic fork in her fingers for a long time.
"For the last five years I've lived with the sense that I'm fatally late for something. Do you understand? Not for a particular train, not for a work meeting. My whole life has turned into an attempt to catch up with something that's already irretrievably gone. Some basic detail I missed right at the start."
I said nothing. Her words had opened up, with surgical precision, the very sensation that had been burning through me all these weeks. We were both passengers running down the platform after a train whose tail lights had long since melted into the dark.
Instead of answering, I silently pushed the flattened receipt with its revealed inscription across to her.
Helen leaned in, peering closely at the grey strokes. She read it twice.
"'If you start to have doubts — stop,'" she whispered, and raised her eyes. "Do you understand what it refers to?"
"Not yet. Right now I doubt absolutely everything, including whether this table is real."
She slowly shook her head:
"And I think I do understand. Your past Michael isn't asking you to stop in the global sense. He's not saying — call off the investigation."
"Then what?"
"He's asking you to stop doubting one particular person. He's putting a block on distrust."
A cold slowly ran down my spine.
"Doubting whom? Harris? You?"
"I don't know," she answered honestly, looking me straight in the eye. "But I think the answer lies much closer than either of us imagines."
We sat at the table a long while more, leaving the cartons where they were. Helen looked out the window. I looked at the receipt. Outside, a night bus passed somewhere — heavy, unhurried, like a departing year.
Then she got up, rinsed her mug, put on her coat. At the threshold she turned back.
"Michael."
"What?"
She was quiet for a second — as if checking whether it was worth saying what she'd meant to.
"You switched your phone off today."
"Yes."
"Good," she nodded — short, serious. "That's the right thing."
And she left. For a few more seconds I looked at the closed door, trying to work out why exactly those two words had sounded like something important. Not praise. Not comfort. Just a quiet, precise statement — as if she knew something I didn't yet know myself.
23:45
Late that night I opened the black notebook again.
I turned the pages slowly, studying the cold, clipped directives. Then my eye happened to slide across the lower right corner of the sheets, where the handwritten numbering ran.
...28, 29, 30, 31...
I turned the page. In the corner of the next spread, in neat ink, was written:
33.
I froze. Slowly went back a step. Turned again. There was no mistake. Between page thirty-one and page thirty-three there was no physical gap. The sheets weren't torn out. There were no traces of a cut or leftover glue at the spine. The binding was intact, the threads pulled evenly.
Page thirty-two didn't exist. It had been absent from the start, at the assembly stage.
I closed my eyes.
The notebook had been bought sealed. A machine at the factory doesn't make numbering errors — because factory notebooks come with no page markings at all. The digits had been entered by a human hand. The past Michael Lawson had personally sat over this notebook and deliberately stepped over one number.
And then a thought pierced me — so simple and mathematically elegant that I was amazed I hadn't got to it earlier.
If he had my level of systems thinking — and he did, that was obvious from every directive after page thirty — then he wasn't just leaving breadcrumbs. He was designing this paper medium as a self-contained instruction with built-in redundancy. He knew with engineering precision that a day would come when the Protocol would crack open this hiding place. That one specific page would be liquidated. And he'd simply built that loss into the architecture of the system in advance. So that I would register the very fact of the deletion. So that the absence would become evidence.
This wasn't a diary. It was a fault-tolerant system, designed for a hostile environment.
I laid my palm on the notebook's black cover and sat motionless for a long time — listening to the ticking of the clock on the wall, the distant noise of the street, my own breathing.
Through all these weeks I had feared the Protocol. Feared the intelligence services, other people's hands in my archives, invisible agents with the authority to clean up other people's lives. Then I'd started fearing my memory. Then — my past self.
But now, in the night silence of the empty flat, the fear finally took a different form. Not a paralyzing one, but a working one.
I no longer wanted to understand who was to blame. I wanted to understand the rules of the game of the man who had designed the present-day me. To run his algorithm to the end — not because I had to, but because it was the only solution the past Michael Lawson had left me as a way out with dignity.
I accepted it.
I slowly opened the notebook to a blank page — the very one that came right after page thirty-three. I took the pen.
And I wrote one line. No directives, no cipher, no instructions. Just for myself — for the Michael who would one day find this notebook and start reading from the beginning.
"I understand the rules. Now I play."
